495	Discussion
496	
497	       The present investigation demonstrated a 100% return-to-play rate after hip or core injury
498	
499	for NFL players. Defensive players with a either a hip or core injury demonstrated significantly
500	
501	fewer games played and both offensive and defensive players experienced decreased power
502	
503	ratings post-injury compared to before injury. Compared to healthy controls, defensive athletes
504	
505	played in significantly fewer games in the two years following injury but returned to near
506	
507	baseline at long term career follow up. Defensive players who sustained hip injuries alone had
508	
509	significantly decreased games played and power ratings in their post-injury careers compared to
510	
511	prior. Offensive players who sustained a core injury had significantly fewer games played in
512	
513	their cumulative career following injury compared to healthy controls.
514	
515	       Hip and groin injuries occur frequently in football players and are a leading cause of
516	
517	injury and lost playing time during both practice and games. [19] In a descriptive epidemiologic
518	
519	study of 23,806 NFL injuries from 1997 to 2006, Feeley et al. found that injuries around the hip
520	
521	comprised 3.1% of total injuries, with muscle strains being the most common. Wide receivers
522	
523	(39.6% of offensive injuries) and defensive backs (47.1% of defensive injuries) were among the
524	
525	most affected by these injuries. [10] The present study found a nearly identical incidence of
526	
527	injury, with wide receivers accounting for 37% of offensive injuries and defensive backs 46% of
528	
529	defensive injuries, with all athletes able to RTP.
530	
531	       High rates of hip and groin injury have also been documented in National Collegiate
532	
533	Athletic Association (NCAA) football players. Kerbel et al reviewed the incidence of hip and
534	
535	groin injuries across multiple sports and found that football players sustained 62.7 hip or groin
536	                                                                                                    13
537	 injuries per 100,000 athlete exposures, with the majority of reported injuries to either the
538	
539	adductor or hip flexor musculature.[20] Specifically investigating muscular strains about the hip,
540	
541	Eckard et al reviewed groin injuries in NCAA athletes and found that hip flexor and adductor
542	
543	muscles strains occurred at a rate of 1.93 and 1.43 per 10,000 athletic exposures in football
544	
545	players, respectively.[21] The present cohort similarly revealed groin or hip flexor strain/tear as
546	
547	among the most common injury type, comprising 56.1% of offensive and 67.6% of defensive
548	
549	injuries. Eckard et al also found 7.4% and 6.9% recurrence rate of hip flexor and adductor strains
550	
551	during the study period, compared to 9.8% of all athletes in our cohort with a documented re-
552	
553	injury.[21] Adductor strains, specifically, have the potential to alter the mechanics of the anterior
554	
555	musculature about the hip leading to increased risk of future rectus strains or athletic
556	
557	pubalgia.[22] Adductor injuries have been shown to cause significant increases in missed time
558	
559	from sport in other professional leagues. Long term performance and career longevity, however,
560	
561	were not altered. [23] These findings suggest that although muscular strains may appear benign,
562	
563	athletes with these injuries are at risk for future strains and time away from sport. Considering
564	
565	groin injuries cause significant time missed in the NFL and other professional sports, prevention
566	
567	is worth investigating. A study by Tyler et al revealed a dedicated physical therapy program
568	
569	targeted at adductor strengthening was beneficial in decreasing the incidence of groin strains in
570	
571	National Hockey League players; a similar training regimen may be beneficial in the NFL as
572	
573	well. [24]
574	
575	       Little is known about the effect of nonoperative core injuries such as back spasm, core
576	
577	stiffness and oblique strain on NFL players. A study utilizing a convenience sample of 267
578	
579	NCAA football players with lumbar spine injuries found that 59.6% of athletes reporting
580	
581	muscular low back pain or contusion were able to return to sport in less than 24 hours and 72.6%
582	
583	
584	
585	                                                                                                    14
586	 of players who did not return in <24 hours returned within a week of injury.[25] Rebolledo et al
587	
588	examined 214 NFL athletes at the combine and found that 50% had a history of abdominal core
589	
590	or lower extremity muscular injury which was also associated with lower levels of Vitamin D.[9]
591	
592	The effect of back and core injury has also been examined in other professional sports, as Camp
593	
594	et al found that core and back injury accounted for 12% of injuries resulting in missed time in
595	
596	Major League Baseball (MLB).[26] Likewise, Marshall et al found that core injuries in MLB
597	
598	pitchers lead to 47.0 ± 5.6 days on the injured list with fewer strikeouts per nine innings in the
599	
600	year of injury.[16] In the our study, athletes sustaining a core injury missed an average of 4.8 ±
601	
602	5.9 games following these injuries and all athletes were able to RTP without significant
603	
604	performance detriment. Additionally, offensive players who suffered a core injury played
605	
606	significantly fewer games throughout the remainder of their post-injury career compared to
607	
608	healthy controls, which could be partially attributed to similarities in athletic demand between a
609	
610	quarterback and MLB pitcher. While return to play rates are high and the current literature does
611	
612	not report significant changes in football performance, Domb et al reviewed disability claims in
613	
614	retired NFL athletes and found that 63 of 65 former players reported symptomatic lumbar spine
615	
616	strain. [27] It is important to note that, while core, and more specifically lumbar spine strains
617	
618	may not be associated with any surgical pathology, the repetitive stress can have implications on
619	
620	the future health of the athlete.
621	
622	        Specifically evaluating hip injuries in the NFL, Feeley et al noted that athletes lost an
623	
624	average of 12.3 days, with a median loss time of 4 days following a variety of hip injuries, such
625	
626	as muscle strains, contusions, and intra-articular pathology.[10] In the aforementioned study by
627	
628	Marshall et al, pitchers with hip injuries spent an average of 37.7 ± 8.1 days on the injured list
629	
630	and starting pitchers suffered from decreased fastball velocity during their initial season
631	
632	
633	                                                                                                     15
634	 following injury.[16] Additionally, injuries around the hip joint have also been shown to lead to
635	
636	missed time in professional basketball, as Jackson et al reviewed 24 years of data and found that
637	
638	hip injury accounted for 14.6% of all athletic injuries and lead to an average of 6.3 ± 10.2 days
639	
640	missed. [28] In our investigation, defensive players were more affected by hip injury than core
641	
642	injuries, with individual decreases in DPR following a hip injury but not a core injury, as well as
643	
644	fewer games played in the two years following injury compared to healthy controls.
645	
646	       Although both offensive skilled players and defensive players saw a decrease in power
647	
648	ratings compared to their own previous performance, neither group experienced a significant
649	
650	decline in performance compared to the control group following a hip or core injury. In a 2017
651	
652	review of player injuries at the NFL combine, Beaulieu-Jones et al. demonstrated that among
653	
654	NFL athletes entering the draft, defensive players with an injury history played fewer games in
655	
656	their first two years in the league compared to healthy controls (22.2 ± 7.9 vs 24.2 ± 7.6 games;
657	
658	p=0.001). Similarly, our study demonstrated that defensive players who suffered a hip or core
659	
660	injury played in fewer games the two years following compared to healthy defensive controls.
661	
662	Additionally, a systematic review by Wang et al looked at 32 studies pertaining to injury
663	
664	surveillance and monitoring at the NFL combine and found that overall, defensive linemen and
665	
666	defensive backs appeared to have their game participation most affected by an injury history
667	
668	compared to offensive athletes.[3] This is likely due to the inherently violent nature of defensive
669	
670	play as compared to offensive play, which predisposes defensive players to more energy transfer
671	
672	and higher impact, and thus higher injury rate. The defensive back position involves more
673	
674	efficient energy transfer in the kinetic chain during movements like backpedaling, quick
675	
676	reactionary changes in direction, and regular high-speed contact, which may help to explain the
677	
678	higher incidence of hip injuries among defensive players. However, it is important to note that in
679	
680	
681	                                                                                                    16
682	 the present investigation performance decline following an injury was not significantly different
683	
684	for offensive skilled or defensive players when comparing to matched controls, thus while
685	
686	athletes may expect some decrease in individual performance, it will not statistically exceed
687	
688	other NFL players of similar age and position.
689	
690	       Our study is not without limitations. Player injury reports were collected from publicly
691	
692	available internet sources which may be subject to inaccuracies. However, the NFL mandates
693	
694	that teams provide accurate and prompt injury information to the league as well as the media.
695	
696	Similar to previous investigations, injuries reports were confirmed with additional publicly
697	
698	available injury reports. [13, 14, 15] With pressure to stay in the game and continue playing,
699	
700	these injuries may also be unreported, as players might not disclose injuries to the team, medical
701	
702	staff and media. Furthermore, while game statistics are an important indicator of player
703	
704	performance, there are many unmeasured contributions not captured, thus true “performance” of
705	
706	a player cannot be completely summarized by these statistics alone. Our use of player power
707	
708	rating attempts to mitigate this issue by generating a weighted value that emphasizes commonly
709	
710	agreed upon significant performance variables.[17] These power ratings, however, do not
711	
712	capture kicker or offensive linemen contributions, therefore these players were excluded from
713	
714	power rating analysis. In addition, hip and core injuries include a broad spectrum of pathologies,
715	
716	and public injury reports often do not indicate the specific diagnosis. We are unable to access
717	
718	clinical exam findings, subjective reports from the athlete, imaging results, and attempted
719	
720	conservative treatment modalities. Future studies should aim to identify specific features that
721	
722	favor successful nonoperative management of common hip and core injuries and correlate with
723	
724	performance.
725	
726	
727	
728	Conclusion
729	                                                                                                  17
730	        Overall, 100% of NFL players in our study returned to play following nonoperative hip
731	
732	and core injuries. Defensive players were more affected post-injury compared to offensive
733	
734	players. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared to core injuries in
735	
736	defensive athletes; offensive athletes played fewer games upon return from core injury but were
737	
738	able to maintain their performance. At long term follow up, both offensive and defensive players
739	
740	were able to return to near baseline games played and power ratings.

                                                                                              2
 The Impact of Non-Operative Hip and Core Injuries on National Football

                     League Athlete Performance




                                                                         3
 Abstract

Objectives: Hip and core injuries are common in National Football League (NFL) athletes;

however, the impact following injury remains unclear. The goal of this manuscript is to

determine the impact of nonoperative hip and core injuries on return to play and performance.

Methods: NFL athletes who sustained a hip or core injury treated non-operatively between 2010-

2016 were identified. Offensive and defensive power ratings were calculated for each player’s

injury season and 2 seasons before and after to assess longitudinal impact. A matched control

group without an identified hip and/or core injury were assembled for comparison.

Results: A total of 41 offensive and 71 defensive players with nonoperative hip or core injury

were analyzed. All athletes returned to play; offensive and defensive players missed 4.0 ± 5.2

and 3.1 ± 2.6 games after injury, respectively. Offensive players played fewer cumulative career

games returning from core injury versus hip (23.5 ± 20.6 vs 41.0 ± 26.4). Defensive players

played fewer games (58.1 ± 41.1 versus 37.4 ± 27.1, p<0.05) with lower defensive power rating

(133.9 ± 128.5 versus 219.8 ± 212.2, p<0.05) cumulatively after hip or core injury. Additionally,

two years following injury, defensive players played fewer games compared to controls (9.5 ±

7.0 versus 10.9 ± 6.8, p<0.05). Following hip injury specifically, NFL defenders played fewer

games (39.8 ± 27.9 vs 61.9 ± 38.8; p<0.05) and had a lower defensive power rating (145.9 ±

131.7 vs 239.0 ± 205.9; p<0.05) compared to before injury.

Conclusion: Overall, NFL players return to play following nonoperative hip and core injuries.

Defensive players played in fewer games following hip or core injury compared to controls;

offensive players were unaffected. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared

to core injuries in defensive athletes; offensive players played fewer games upon return from

core injury.

                                                                                                 4
 Key Terms: Muscle injuries, football, groin pain, hip/pelvis/thigh, core




                                                                           5
 Introduction

       Injuries in the National Football League (NFL) have been shown to have a significant

financial burden to both players and organizations.[1, 2] A systematic review of athletes entering

the NFL combine with a musculoskeletal injury that required orthopedic intervention are

uniformly at risk for decreased performance and fewer games, the effects of which resonate

throughout an NFL player’s career.[3, 4] Although knee and shoulder injury account for the

highest incidence of time loss injuries among NFL players, they are at significant risk for injuries

to other anatomic regions, particularly the hip and core.[5, 6, 7, 8]

       Hip and core injuries in the NFL account for approximately 10% of NFL injuries; the

majority are classified as muscle strains. [9, 10] In fact, hip flexor strains occurred 268 times

over a 10 year period in the NFL, and were the most common hip injury. [10] Football players

are particularly vulnerable to core injuries such as rib fractures or contusions, back stiffness as

well as abdominal/oblique strains, and athletic pubalgia due to the physical nature of the game.

[11, 12] Prior studies have examined the effect of surgical intervention on groin injuries,

showing that operative intervention for athletica pubalgia led to significantly shorter career

length and games per season compared to matched controls,[13] however the impact of

nonoperative hip and core injuries on NFL player performance has not been elucidated.

       The purpose of our investigation was to determine the impact of nonoperative hip and

core injuries on the performance in NFL athletes. We sought to determine if these injuries had a

significant impact on return to play rates, as well as offensive and defensive player productivity.

It was hypothesized that both offensive and defensive NFL players who sustained a nonoperative

hip or core injury would return to play but play fewer games and experience worse performance

following their return as compared to healthy controls matched for age, position, and NFL

experience.
                                                                                                      6
 Methods

       Data were collected retrospectively for this study; internal review board exemption was

granted since all material is freely accessible. All NFL players who sustained a hip or core injury

between 2010-2016 seasons were collected from publicly available sources such as injury

reports, player profiles, team pages and game summaries using methods previously utilized in

other studies.[13, 14, 15, 16] Indexed hip injuries included adductor strain, hip flexor strain,

labral tears, hip inflammation or impingement while core injuries included oblique, abdominal or

intercostal strains, as well as back spasms or stiffness. Injuries were cross referenced with public

websites including official team pages, official press releases, and personal player websites,

using methodology that has been utilized by previous studies using publicly available

databases.[13, 14, 15, 16] The NFL mandates that teams quickly and accurately disseminate

injury information to the league office, their opponents, local and national media, and the team’s

broadcast partners. Return-to-play (RTP) data was further confirmed by identifying gaps in

reported statistics. Fractures, disc herniations, and any player who was reported to have

undergone surgery for their injury were not included in the investigation.

       Demographic data surrounding the injury were recorded such as BMI, age at injury,

season in NFL that injury occurred and position. The total number of games played before and

after the reported injury date were also recorded. Performance data was collected for each player

including total games played, total yards (passing, rushing or receiving) and touchdowns for

offensive players and total tackles, sacks and interceptions for defensive players. Offensive and

defensive power ratings were also calculated from these variables, which have both been

previously described and validated outcomes measures of a football player’s overall contribution

to the team’s offense or defense.[14, 17, 18] They are calculated with the following formulas:
                                                                                                    7
 Offensive power rating (OPR) = [(total yards/10) + (touchdowns/6)]

Defensive power rating (DPR) = [total tackles + (total sacks x 2) + (total interceptions x 2)]

       Overall career data as well as data in the two years prior to and following the date of

injury were collected in order to better assess longitudinal changes in performance. Power ratings

are intended to calculate productivity over a season, not individual games; therefore, the

individual statistics were also evaluated on a per game basis to account for games missed. A

control group was assembled by 2:1 matching injured athletes with healthy rostered NFL players

that did not sustain a documented hip and/or groin injury by age, position, performance data, and

NFL experience within three seasons in accordance to previously established methodology. [13,

14, 15] Control players were chosen based on an index date which was matched with the study

player’s date of injury. This control group was established to compare performance before and

after hip/core injury. Additionally, if players did not participate in the season prior to the index

injury season they were excluded. Furthermore, athletes injured at the end of the season who

were unable to return-to-play during the index season were excluded from the study. When

calculating time missed from injury, bye weeks were not a factor, only the number of games

missed. Power rating has been previously demonstrated in other investigations to be a valid and

effective method for quantifying overall player performance;[14] however, since several studies

demonstrated offensive power ratings are not an effective performance metric for offensive

linemen (OL) or kickers (K), only offensive skill players (wide receivers [WR], running backs

[RB], tight ends [TE], and quarterbacks [QB]) were included for offensive power ratings.[17, 18]

Statistical Analysis

       All continuous data are reported as mean ± standard deviation, while categorical data are

reported as counts and column percentages. Comparisons between injured and control players


                                                                                                       8
 are performed using independent 2-sample t-tests for continuous variables and using chi-square

tests for categorical variables. Comparisons between pre- and post- data are performed using

paired t-tests if the variable is normally distributed, and Wilcoxon signed rank tests if the

variable is non-normally distributed. Statistical significance is set at p<0.05. All analyses are

performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).



Results

        A total of 112 (41 offensive and 71 defensive) NFL players were identified as having

sustained a hip or core injury between 2010 and 2016 that also matched our inclusion criteria.

The offensive group included 15 wide receivers, 10 offensive linemen, 6 tight ends, 5 running

backs, 4 quarterbacks and 1 kicker. Defensive players included 33 defensive backs, 19

linebackers, 10 defensive ends, and 9 defensive tackles. A 2:1 matched control group consisting

of 224 players was compared to the study group and demonstrated no statistical differences in

age, years of NFL experience, position, or BMI (Table 1). Pre-injury performance did not

significantly differ between the injured group and healthy controls. No players sustained injuries

requiring retirement.

Discussion

       The present investigation demonstrated a 100% return-to-play rate after hip or core injury

for NFL players. Defensive players with a either a hip or core injury demonstrated significantly

fewer games played and both offensive and defensive players experienced decreased power

ratings post-injury compared to before injury. Compared to healthy controls, defensive athletes

played in significantly fewer games in the two years following injury but returned to near

baseline at long term career follow up. Defensive players who sustained hip injuries alone had

significantly decreased games played and power ratings in their post-injury careers compared to

prior. Offensive players who sustained a core injury had significantly fewer games played in

their cumulative career following injury compared to healthy controls.

       Hip and groin injuries occur frequently in football players and are a leading cause of

injury and lost playing time during both practice and games. [19] In a descriptive epidemiologic

study of 23,806 NFL injuries from 1997 to 2006, Feeley et al. found that injuries around the hip

comprised 3.1% of total injuries, with muscle strains being the most common. Wide receivers

(39.6% of offensive injuries) and defensive backs (47.1% of defensive injuries) were among the

most affected by these injuries. [10] The present study found a nearly identical incidence of

injury, with wide receivers accounting for 37% of offensive injuries and defensive backs 46% of

defensive injuries, with all athletes able to RTP.

       High rates of hip and groin injury have also been documented in National Collegiate

Athletic Association (NCAA) football players. Kerbel et al reviewed the incidence of hip and

groin injuries across multiple sports and found that football players sustained 62.7 hip or groin
                                                                                                    13
 injuries per 100,000 athlete exposures, with the majority of reported injuries to either the

adductor or hip flexor musculature.[20] Specifically investigating muscular strains about the hip,

Eckard et al reviewed groin injuries in NCAA athletes and found that hip flexor and adductor

muscles strains occurred at a rate of 1.93 and 1.43 per 10,000 athletic exposures in football

players, respectively.[21] The present cohort similarly revealed groin or hip flexor strain/tear as

among the most common injury type, comprising 56.1% of offensive and 67.6% of defensive

injuries. Eckard et al also found 7.4% and 6.9% recurrence rate of hip flexor and adductor strains

during the study period, compared to 9.8% of all athletes in our cohort with a documented re-

injury.[21] Adductor strains, specifically, have the potential to alter the mechanics of the anterior

musculature about the hip leading to increased risk of future rectus strains or athletic

pubalgia.[22] Adductor injuries have been shown to cause significant increases in missed time

from sport in other professional leagues. Long term performance and career longevity, however,

were not altered. [23] These findings suggest that although muscular strains may appear benign,

athletes with these injuries are at risk for future strains and time away from sport. Considering

groin injuries cause significant time missed in the NFL and other professional sports, prevention

is worth investigating. A study by Tyler et al revealed a dedicated physical therapy program

targeted at adductor strengthening was beneficial in decreasing the incidence of groin strains in

National Hockey League players; a similar training regimen may be beneficial in the NFL as

well. [24]

       Little is known about the effect of nonoperative core injuries such as back spasm, core

stiffness and oblique strain on NFL players. A study utilizing a convenience sample of 267

NCAA football players with lumbar spine injuries found that 59.6% of athletes reporting

muscular low back pain or contusion were able to return to sport in less than 24 hours and 72.6%



                                                                                                    14
 of players who did not return in <24 hours returned within a week of injury.[25] Rebolledo et al

examined 214 NFL athletes at the combine and found that 50% had a history of abdominal core

or lower extremity muscular injury which was also associated with lower levels of Vitamin D.[9]

The effect of back and core injury has also been examined in other professional sports, as Camp

et al found that core and back injury accounted for 12% of injuries resulting in missed time in

Major League Baseball (MLB).[26] Likewise, Marshall et al found that core injuries in MLB

pitchers lead to 47.0 ± 5.6 days on the injured list with fewer strikeouts per nine innings in the

year of injury.[16] In the our study, athletes sustaining a core injury missed an average of 4.8 ±

5.9 games following these injuries and all athletes were able to RTP without significant

performance detriment. Additionally, offensive players who suffered a core injury played

significantly fewer games throughout the remainder of their post-injury career compared to

healthy controls, which could be partially attributed to similarities in athletic demand between a

quarterback and MLB pitcher. While return to play rates are high and the current literature does

not report significant changes in football performance, Domb et al reviewed disability claims in

retired NFL athletes and found that 63 of 65 former players reported symptomatic lumbar spine

strain. [27] It is important to note that, while core, and more specifically lumbar spine strains

may not be associated with any surgical pathology, the repetitive stress can have implications on

the future health of the athlete.

        Specifically evaluating hip injuries in the NFL, Feeley et al noted that athletes lost an

average of 12.3 days, with a median loss time of 4 days following a variety of hip injuries, such

as muscle strains, contusions, and intra-articular pathology.[10] In the aforementioned study by

Marshall et al, pitchers with hip injuries spent an average of 37.7 ± 8.1 days on the injured list

and starting pitchers suffered from decreased fastball velocity during their initial season


                                                                                                     15
 following injury.[16] Additionally, injuries around the hip joint have also been shown to lead to

missed time in professional basketball, as Jackson et al reviewed 24 years of data and found that

hip injury accounted for 14.6% of all athletic injuries and lead to an average of 6.3 ± 10.2 days

missed. [28] In our investigation, defensive players were more affected by hip injury than core

injuries, with individual decreases in DPR following a hip injury but not a core injury, as well as

fewer games played in the two years following injury compared to healthy controls.

       Although both offensive skilled players and defensive players saw a decrease in power

ratings compared to their own previous performance, neither group experienced a significant

decline in performance compared to the control group following a hip or core injury. In a 2017

review of player injuries at the NFL combine, Beaulieu-Jones et al. demonstrated that among

NFL athletes entering the draft, defensive players with an injury history played fewer games in

their first two years in the league compared to healthy controls (22.2 ± 7.9 vs 24.2 ± 7.6 games;

p=0.001). Similarly, our study demonstrated that defensive players who suffered a hip or core

injury played in fewer games the two years following compared to healthy defensive controls.

Additionally, a systematic review by Wang et al looked at 32 studies pertaining to injury

surveillance and monitoring at the NFL combine and found that overall, defensive linemen and

defensive backs appeared to have their game participation most affected by an injury history

compared to offensive athletes.[3] This is likely due to the inherently violent nature of defensive

play as compared to offensive play, which predisposes defensive players to more energy transfer

and higher impact, and thus higher injury rate. The defensive back position involves more

efficient energy transfer in the kinetic chain during movements like backpedaling, quick

reactionary changes in direction, and regular high-speed contact, which may help to explain the

higher incidence of hip injuries among defensive players. However, it is important to note that in


                                                                                                    16
 the present investigation performance decline following an injury was not significantly different

for offensive skilled or defensive players when comparing to matched controls, thus while

athletes may expect some decrease in individual performance, it will not statistically exceed

other NFL players of similar age and position.

       Our study is not without limitations. Player injury reports were collected from publicly

available internet sources which may be subject to inaccuracies. However, the NFL mandates

that teams provide accurate and prompt injury information to the league as well as the media.

Similar to previous investigations, injuries reports were confirmed with additional publicly

available injury reports. [13, 14, 15] With pressure to stay in the game and continue playing,

these injuries may also be unreported, as players might not disclose injuries to the team, medical

staff and media. Furthermore, while game statistics are an important indicator of player

performance, there are many unmeasured contributions not captured, thus true “performance” of

a player cannot be completely summarized by these statistics alone. Our use of player power

rating attempts to mitigate this issue by generating a weighted value that emphasizes commonly

agreed upon significant performance variables.[17] These power ratings, however, do not

capture kicker or offensive linemen contributions, therefore these players were excluded from

power rating analysis. In addition, hip and core injuries include a broad spectrum of pathologies,

and public injury reports often do not indicate the specific diagnosis. We are unable to access

clinical exam findings, subjective reports from the athlete, imaging results, and attempted

conservative treatment modalities. Future studies should aim to identify specific features that

favor successful nonoperative management of common hip and core injuries and correlate with

performance.



Conclusion
                                                                                                  17
        Overall, 100% of NFL players in our study returned to play following nonoperative hip

and core injuries. Defensive players were more affected post-injury compared to offensive

players. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared to core injuries in

defensive athletes; offensive athletes played fewer games upon return from core injury but were

able to maintain their performance. At long term follow up, both offensive and defensive players

were able to return to near baseline games played and power ratings.

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                      ARTICLE HISTORY
    Objectives: Hip and core injuries are common in National Football League (NFL) athletes; however, the                         Received 17 April 2021
    impact following injury remains unclear. The goal of this manuscript was to determine the impact of                           Accepted 21 August 2021
    nonoperative hip and core injuries on return to play and performance.
                                                                                                                                  KEYWORDS
    Methods: NFL athletes who sustained a hip or core injury treated nonoperatively between 2010 and
                                                                                                                                  Muscle injuries; football;
    2016 were identified. Offensive and defensive power ratings were calculated for each player’s injury                          groin pain; hip/pelvis/thigh;
    season and two seasons before and after to assess longitudinal impact. A matched control group                                core
    without an identified hip and/or core injury was assembled for comparison.
    Results: A total of 41 offensive and 71 defensive players with nonoperative hip or core injury were
    analyzed. All athletes returned to play; offensive and defensive players missed 4.0 ± 5.2 and 3.1 ± 2.6
    games after injury, respectively. Offensive players played fewer cumulative career games returning from
    core injury versus hip (23.5 ± 20.6 vs 41.0 ± 26.4). Defensive players played fewer games (58.1 ± 41.1
    versus 37.4 ± 27.1, p < 0.05) with lower defensive power rating (133.9 ± 128.5 versus 219.8 ± 212.2,
    p < 0.05) cumulatively after hip or core injury. Additionally, 2 years following injury, defensive players
    played fewer games compared to controls (9.5 ± 7.0 versus 10.9 ± 6.8, p < 0.05). Following hip injury
    specifically, NFL defenders played fewer games (39.8 ± 27.9 vs 61.9 ± 38.8; p < 0.05) and had a lower
    defensive power rating (145.9 ± 131.7 vs 239.0 ± 205.9; p < 0.05) compared to before injury.
    Conclusion: Overall, NFL players return to play following nonoperative hip and core injuries. Defensive
    players played in fewer games following hip or core injury compared to controls; offensive players were
    unaffected. Hip injuries have a greater impact on performance compared to core injuries in defensive
    athletes; offensive players played fewer games upon return from core injury.

16	  Abstract
17	  Background Sleep is essential for maximal performance in the athletic population. Despite that, the sport context
18	  has many factors that can negatively influence athletes’ sleep and subsequent recovery.
19	  Objectives The purpose of this systematic review was to synthesize the most recent literature regarding sleep inter-
20	  ventions aimed at improving sleep and subsequent performance in athletes.
21	  Methods The present systematic review was conducted based on the PRISMA guidelines and the PICOS approach.
22	  The search was conducted in May 2022 using the electronic database PubMed, SPORTDiscus via EBSCOhost, and Web
23	  of Science. Once extracted, studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) participants were athletes
24	  of individual or team sports; (2) implemented an intervention aimed at improving sleep; (3) measured at least one
25	  objective performance/recovery outcome; and (4) reported the relationship between sleep and performance.
26	  Results The search returned 1584 records. Following the screening, a total of 25 studies met our inclusion criteria. All
27	  the included articles were intervention studies published between 2011 and 2021. The included studies implemented
28	  various sleep interventions, such as sleep hygiene, naps, sleep extension, light manipulation, cold water immersion,
29	  mindfulness, or a combination of two or more strategies. Sleep extension and naps were the most representative
30	  and most effective strategies to improve sleep and performance. Mindfulness and light manipulation demonstrated
31	  promising results, but more studies are needed to confirm these findings. Sleep hygiene, removing electronic devices
32	  at night, and cold water immersion had no effects on sleep and subsequent performance/recovery, but these results
33	  are based on a few studies only.
34	  Conclusion While acknowledging the limited amount of high-quality evidence reviewed, it appears that increasing
35	  sleep duration at night or through napping was the most effective interventions to improve physical and/or cognitive
36	  performance.
37	  Protocol Registration This protocol was registered in the International Platform of Registered Systematic Review
38	  and Meta-Analysis Protocols (INPLASY) on May 11, 2022, with the registration number INPLASY202250069.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW                                                                                                                                             Open Access

The Impact of Sleep Interventions
on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review
Lúcio A. Cunha1 , Júlio A. Costa2 , Elisa A. Marques1,3 , João Brito2 , Michele Lastella4    and
Pedro Figueiredo5,6*   



  Abstract
  Background Sleep is essential for maximal performance in the athletic population. Despite that, the sport context
  has many factors that can negatively influence athletes’ sleep and subsequent recovery.
  Objectives The purpose of this systematic review was to synthesize the most recent literature regarding sleep inter-
  ventions aimed at improving sleep and subsequent performance in athletes.
  Methods The present systematic review was conducted based on the PRISMA guidelines and the PICOS approach.
  The search was conducted in May 2022 using the electronic database PubMed, SPORTDiscus via EBSCOhost, and Web
  of Science. Once extracted, studies were included if they met the following criteria: (1) participants were athletes
  of individual or team sports; (2) implemented an intervention aimed at improving sleep; (3) measured at least one
  objective performance/recovery outcome; and (4) reported the relationship between sleep and performance.
  Results The search returned 1584 records. Following the screening, a total of 25 studies met our inclusion criteria. All
  the included articles were intervention studies published between 2011 and 2021. The included studies implemented
  various sleep interventions, such as sleep hygiene, naps, sleep extension, light manipulation, cold water immersion,
  mindfulness, or a combination of two or more strategies. Sleep extension and naps were the most representative
  and most effective strategies to improve sleep and performance. Mindfulness and light manipulation demonstrated
  promising results, but more studies are needed to confirm these findings. Sleep hygiene, removing electronic devices
  at night, and cold water immersion had no effects on sleep and subsequent performance/recovery, but these results
  are based on a few studies only.
  Conclusion While acknowledging the limited amount of high-quality evidence reviewed, it appears that increasing
  sleep duration at night or through napping was the most effective interventions to improve physical and/or cognitive
  performance.
  Protocol Registration This protocol was registered in the International Platform of Registered Systematic Review
  and Meta-Analysis Protocols (INPLASY) on May 11, 2022, with the registration number INPLASY202250069.
  Keywords Sleep interventions, Athletes, Performance

10	1RM prediction using the load-velocity

12	Mark G. L. Sayers1* , Michel Schlaeppi2, Marina Hitz2 and Silvio Lorenzetti2,3
13	
14	
15	  Abstract
16	  Background: Numerous methods have been proposed that use submaximal loads to predict one repetition
17	  maximum (1RM). One common method applies standard linear regression equations to load and average vertical
18	  lifting velocity (Vmean) data developed during squat jumps or three bench press throw (BP-T). The main aim of this
19	  project was to determine which combination of three submaximal loads during BP-T result in the most accurate
20	  prediction of 1RM Smith Machine bench press strength in healthy individuals.
21	  Methods: In this study combinations of three BP-T loads were used to predict 1RM Smith Machine bench press
22	  strength. Additionally, we examined whether regression models developed using peak vertical bar velocity (Vpeak),
23	  rather than Vmean, provide the most accurate prediction of Smith Machine bench press 1RM. 1RM Smith Machine
24	  bench press strength was measured directly in 12 healthy regular weight trainers (body mass = 80.8 ± 5.7 kg). Two
25	  to three days later a linear position transducer attached to the collars on a Smith Machine was used to record
26	  Vmean and Vpeak during BP-T between 30 and 70% of 1RM (10% increments).
27	  Results: Repeated measures analysis of variance testing showed that the mean values for slope and ordinate
28	  intercept for the regression models at each of the load ranges differed significantly depending on whether Vmean or
29	  Vpeak were used in the prediction models (P < 0.001). Conversely, the abscissa intercept did not differ significantly
30	  between either measure of vertical bar velocity at each load range. The key finding in this study was that 1RM
31	  Smith Machine bench press strength can be determined with high relative accuracy by examining Vmean and Vpeak
32	  during BP-T over three loads, with the most precise models using Vpeak during loads representing 30, 40 and 50%
33	  of 1RM (R2 = 0.96, SSE = 4.2 kg).
34	  Conclusions: These preliminary findings indicate that exercise programmers working with normal healthy
35	  populations can accurately predict Smith Machine 1RM bench press strength using relatively light load Smith
36	  Machine BP-T testing, avoiding the need to expose their clients to potentially injurious loads.
37	  Keywords: Strength assessment, Dynamic strength, Predictive models, Bench press throws

The impact of test loads on the accuracy of
1RM prediction using the load-velocity
relationship
Mark G. L. Sayers1* , Michel Schlaeppi2, Marina Hitz2 and Silvio Lorenzetti2,3


  Abstract
  Background: Numerous methods have been proposed that use submaximal loads to predict one repetition
  maximum (1RM). One common method applies standard linear regression equations to load and average vertical
  lifting velocity (Vmean) data developed during squat jumps or three bench press throw (BP-T). The main aim of this
  project was to determine which combination of three submaximal loads during BP-T result in the most accurate
  prediction of 1RM Smith Machine bench press strength in healthy individuals.
  Methods: In this study combinations of three BP-T loads were used to predict 1RM Smith Machine bench press
  strength. Additionally, we examined whether regression models developed using peak vertical bar velocity (Vpeak),
  rather than Vmean, provide the most accurate prediction of Smith Machine bench press 1RM. 1RM Smith Machine
  bench press strength was measured directly in 12 healthy regular weight trainers (body mass = 80.8 ± 5.7 kg). Two
  to three days later a linear position transducer attached to the collars on a Smith Machine was used to record
  Vmean and Vpeak during BP-T between 30 and 70% of 1RM (10% increments).
  Results: Repeated measures analysis of variance testing showed that the mean values for slope and ordinate
  intercept for the regression models at each of the load ranges differed significantly depending on whether Vmean or
  Vpeak were used in the prediction models (P < 0.001). Conversely, the abscissa intercept did not differ significantly
  between either measure of vertical bar velocity at each load range. The key finding in this study was that 1RM
  Smith Machine bench press strength can be determined with high relative accuracy by examining Vmean and Vpeak
  during BP-T over three loads, with the most precise models using Vpeak during loads representing 30, 40 and 50%
  of 1RM (R2 = 0.96, SSE = 4.2 kg).
  Conclusions: These preliminary findings indicate that exercise programmers working with normal healthy
  populations can accurately predict Smith Machine 1RM bench press strength using relatively light load Smith
  Machine BP-T testing, avoiding the need to expose their clients to potentially injurious loads.
  Keywords: Strength assessment, Dynamic strength, Predictive models, Bench press throws

14	                                          Abstract: While velocity-based training is currently a very popular paradigm to designing and
15	                                          monitoring resistance training programs, its implementation remains a challenge in team sports,
16	                                          where there are still some confusion and misinterpretations of its applications. In addition, in contexts
17	                                          with large squads, it is paramount to understand how to best use movement velocity in different
18	                                          exercises in a useful and time-efficient way. This manuscript aims to provide clarifications on the
19	                                          velocity-based training paradigm, movement velocity tracking technologies, assessment procedures
20	                                          and practical recommendations for its application during resistance training sessions, with the
21	                                          purpose of increasing performance, managing fatigue and preventing injuries. Guidelines to combine
22	                                          velocity metrics with subjective scales to prescribe training loads are presented, as well as methods
23	          
24	                                   to estimate 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM) on a daily basis using individual load–velocity profiles.
25	Citation: Balsalobre-Fernández, C.;       Additionally, monitoring strategies to detect and evaluate changes in performance over time are
26	Torres-Ronda, L. The Implementation       discussed. Finally, limitations regarding the use of velocity of execution tracking devices and metrics

28	for Team Sports: Framework,

30	Recommendations and Challenges.
31	Sports 2021, 9, 47. https://doi.org/
32	10.3390/sports9040047
33	
34	                                          1. Introduction
35	Academic Editor: Corrado Lupo
36	                                                The importance of resistance training (RT) in team sports, either due to the extensive
37	                                          scientific (and empirical) justification, or its impact in improving overall performance [1,2],
38	Received: 8 March 2021
39	Accepted: 29 March 2021
40	                                          as well as on minimizing injury risk and in the return-to-play [3,4], is unquestionable. As
41	Published: 30 March 2021
42	                                          in other fields, technology can be a source of support, progress and innovation in the RT
43	                                          methodology. However, the advancement in technology for the programming, control and

46	with regard to jurisdictional claims in
47	                                          ology, or the best practices of its implementation. The information provided by certain
48	published maps and institutional affil-   RT tracking systems can have a great impact on the programming and control of training,
49	iations.                                  but especially, on the evaluation and criticism of the training methodology implemented.
50	                                          Thereby, coaches (e.g., strength and conditioning coaches (S&C), physiotherapists) can
51	                                          obtain objective information to analyze whether they are achieving the desired results with
52	                                          their program, how the improvements (or setbacks) occur, and thus, can improve their
53	Copyright: © 2021 by the authors.
54	                                          general knowledge of the strength training paradigm.
55	Licensee MDPI, Basel, Switzerland.
56	                                                Two of the most frequent indicators used as a reference to prescribe RT have been
57	This article is an open access article
58	                                          the 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM) and the maximum number of repetitions at a given
59	distributed under the terms and           percentage of this weight (n1RM%) [5,6]. However, despite being useful to some extent
60	conditions of the Creative Commons        for an apparent individualization of training, these procedures present limitations that
61	Attribution (CC BY) license (https://     made the scientific and applied community explore other strategies, leading to the design
62	creativecommons.org/licenses/by/          of strength training programs. A still emerging method, although not new, is the velocity-
63	4.0/).                                    based training (VBT), representing both a less invasive and a more optimal method to
64	
65	
66	
67	Sports 2021, 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.3390/sports9040047                                                       https://www.mdpi.com/journal/sports
68	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                            2 of 14
69	
70	
71	
72	                     prescribe RT based on velocity of execution. This is a key element in most sport disciplines,
73	                     either by the requirements of the sport (e.g., sprinting, accelerating/decelerating, jumping,
74	                     throwing, kicking) or as an indicator of intensity (e.g., neuromuscular demands) [7,8].
75	                     There are reports of German weightlifters using linear transducers in the 1970s [9]. Since
76	                     that time, research on the benefits of lifting velocity to prescribe and monitor RT has
77	                     been conducted [8,10–12]. Being able to objectively monitor RT sessions, adapt the goals
78	                     individually, or provide feedback in real time on a daily basis is paramount, especially when
79	                     working with elite players. In addition, compiling information will allow a critical analysis
80	                     based on objective data on the implemented methodology, and thus enable the necessary
81	                     adjustments and advancements in the knowledge of the strength training theory. However,
82	                     there are still some confusion, misinterpretations and wrong practices when implementing
83	                     VBT in team sports. Therefore, the aim of this article is to provide a comprehensive
84	                     overview of the main benefits, technologies and best practices when implementing VBT
85	                     programs in team sports.
86	
87	                     2. The Challenges and Drawbacks of the 1-Repetition Maximum Paradigm
88	                          The value of 1RM represents the maximal load (mass) that the athlete can lift, in a
89	                     concentric dynamic action, with proper form, once but not twice [13]. Thus, performing
90	                     a 1RM is considered a maximal dynamic effort. Once this value is known, programming
91	                     of RT is done prescribing relative loads to the individual’s 1RM [14,15]. However, this
92	                     methodology comes with certain disadvantages.
93	                          It is well known in the powerlifting community that experienced lifters are able
94	                     to move their 1RM load (mass) at a lower speed than their less trained or experienced
95	                     counterparts, especially in complex multi-joint exercises. Either due to inexperience, not
96	                     making a truly maximum effort or having experience but avoiding situations of risk of
97	                     injury using maximum loads, the 1RM is often poorly measured, which implies that the
98	                     consequent prescribed load (percentage-based training; nRM%), or velocities for each
99	                     1RM%, will not be adequate.
100	                          Moreover, as happens with other measures of physical performance, the 1RM could
101	                     vary on a daily basis due to several uncontrolled factors (e.g., fatigue, mental preparation,
102	                     sleep, stress or nutrition) [16]. Hence, in order to prescribe a precise load for each session,
103	                     the 1RM should be tested at the beginning of every RT session to adjust loads to the actual
104	                     (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete. However, since conducting an actual
105	                     1RM test before each training session is utopic, traditional percentage-based approaches
106	                     have been used, where the 1RM is assessed at the beginning of a training cycle, the %RM is
107	                     calculated and the RT program periodized for the subsequent weeks according to it [12,17].
108	                     The main drawback with this approach is that, since the actual 1RM could vary from
109	                     one session to another, the subsequent prescribed loads (mass) for the cycle would likely
110	                     represent a different effort to the initial loads (%RM) programed based on the original 1RM.
111	                     As an illustration of this potential discrepancy, Table 1 displays a RT load progression over
112	                     a period of 8-weeks, with one example based on the 1RM assessed prior to the training
113	                     cycle, and an example based on daily estimations using load–velocity profiles.
114	                          Additionally, the effort that represents each 1RM percentage differs between exer-
115	                     cises [18,19], where, for example, the 85% 1RM represents a different effort in bench press
116	                     vs. back squat. Furthermore, the load that represents a %1RM still requires performing
117	                     repetitions to failure, and extensive research has shown that performing repetitions to mus-
118	                     cular failure can impair performance, at specific times of a periodization program, due to an
119	                     excessive production of fatigue, thus making it inappropriate for team sports training [20].
120	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                                  3 of 14
121	
122	
123	
124	      Table 1. Comparison of the load associated with 70% 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM), using the pre-test value (session 1) or
125	      actual daily values.
126	
127	                            Session 1        Session 2       Session 3       Session 4       Session 5       Session 6       Session 7        Session 8
128	      1RM (kg)                  130              —               —               —               —                —               —               —
129	   Load @ 70%1RM
130	                                 91              91              91              91              91               91              91              91
131	        (kg)
132	  Actual daily 1RM              130            132.5            130              135            137.5           132.5            135             140
133	  Load @ 70% 1RM
134	                                 91            92.75             91             94.5            96.25           92.75            94.5             98
135	        (kg)
136	      In the pretest session (i.e., Session 0), the 1RM of the athlete represented in this table was 130 kg in the bench-press exercise. Those 130 kg
137	      were used as a reference in the “pretest programming”, while daily 1RM scores estimated by measuring barbell velocity were used in the
138	      “daily programming”. Note that in the pre-test programming, every session would have been performed with 91 kg (i.e., the 70% of the
139	      pre-test 1RM), but if daily variations would have been taken into account, the actual load would have variated on a daily basis.
140	
141	
142	                                      3. Technologies to Track Velocity for Resistance Training
143	                                            Due to the growing interest in VBT, there has been a proliferation of devices measuring
144	                                      velocity for RT, from motion capture systems (MoCap), linear transducers and accelerome-
145	                                      ters, to low-cost smartphone apps. In addition, this phenomenon has been accompanied
146	                                      by a number of studies conducted on the validity and reliability of some of these novel
147	                                      technologies to measure velocity [21–29]. However, each of these technologies has advan-
148	                                      tages and disadvantages, and practitioners tasked with managing the systems have the
149	                                      responsibility to understand the pros and cons of the different systems, as well as using a
150	                                      systematic process in the data collection, being knowledgeable on best practices regarding
151	                                      implementing VBT, and applying critical thinking when assessing their RT methodologies.
152	                                            Team sports rarely require static, linear or single-joint movements. Rather, it is the
153	                                      opposite in that there are not only complex movements but also ones performed in highly
154	                                      unpredictable environments and with opponents (involving contact, perturbations, colli-
155	                                      sions, and such). Velocity tracking systems are still far from being able to measure with
156	                                      ecological validity; most are designed to measure traditional strength exercises, connected
157	                                      to equipment, or to certain body segments.
158	                                            Linear transducers are probably one of the most popular technologies used in the
159	                                      implementation of VBT to date. One of the downsides is that they are limited to measure
160	                                      vertical motion only [30,31]. Most commercial models available in the market just measure
161	                                      the vertical component of the velocity vector, meaning that any horizontal or lateral motion
162	                                      during the lift would be (and should be) omitted (Figure 1). Horizontal displacements
163	                                      do occur when using free weights even in “vertical” exercises like the back squat [32,33];
164	                                      hence, a proper exercise form and technique should be guaranteed, and exercises with a
165	                                      horizontal or angular momentum component avoided.
166	                                            In most cases, linear transducers are attached to one end of a barbell, and thus they
167	                                      actually register the velocity of that part of the bar, which could differ from the velocity
168	                                      of the other end if the athlete did not lift it perfectly, parallel to the ground. Lifting an
169	                                      unbalanced barbell does happen in practice, and S&C coaches using linear transducers
170	                                      should be aware of this fact. To reduce this type of error in the measurement, some studies
171	                                      have used two linear transducers, and reported the mean velocity registered from the two
172	                                      devices [30,32]. This may not be feasible in applied contexts; an alternative support may
173	                                      be having a visual control of the form of execution (objective or subjective) and exclude
174	                                      incorrect repetitions. It is then recommended that the device is placed consistently on the
175	                                      same side.
176	                                            Trying to solve some of the aforementioned limitations, different novel technologies
177	                                      such as accelerometers or smartphone apps have emerged as a cost-effective and prac-
178	                                      tical alternative to measure movement velocity in resistance exercises, and studies have
179	                                      shown that they can do it in a valid and reliable way [22,25,28,34]. For example, certain
180	                                      accelerometers can track velocity in exercises with horizontal displacement, while apps
181	                                      have shown reliable measurement of mean concentric velocity in cable-based exercises
182	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                   4 of 14
183	
184	
185	
186	                     by video-recording the vertical ascent of the machine’s weight stack [35]. However, these
187	                     devices come with their own limitations. While they have shown moderate to good validity
188	                     and reliability, accelerometers had the lowest accuracy when compared with other devices,
189	                     such as linear transducers, apps, MoCap or gold-standard instruments [22,28]. A popular
190	                     app [25] has presented validity, reliability and accuracy higher than accelerometers; how-
191	                     ever, since it is video-based (frame-to-frame slow motion navigation), the measurements
192	                     are not provided in real time. When comparing different linear transducers, studies have
193	                     observed differences in absolute velocity outputs [28]. Thus, when interpreting VBT re-
194	                     search (especially when looking to raw velocity data) practitioners should interpret results
195	                     carefully; it is advised to not use devices from different manufactures interchangeably.
196	
197	
198	
199	
200	                     Figure 1. Generic linear transducer showing a deviation of 20◦ from the vertical during a lift.
201	                     For a registered mean velocity of 0.82 m·s−1 , the actual magnitude of the resultant mean velocity
202	                     vector would be 0.87 m/s, as calculated using simple trigonometry (Actual velocity = Registered
203	                     velocity/cos (angle). Most of the load–velocity relationships analyzed in the scientific literature are
204	                     conducted with exercises performed in Smith machines, since this equipment guarantees a complete
205	                     vertical motion of the barbell. This, however, reduces the ecological validity of the load–velocity
206	                     relationship itself, since these profiles can differ if the lift is performed with free weights (where
207	                     horizontal displacements occur) or with a Smith machine.
208	
209	                           Another common misappropriation of technologies to track movement velocity is
210	                     its application for the measurement of power or “muscle power”. Power is important in
211	                     sport because it is an expression of performance, the consequence of the force applied in a
212	                     given time in a given action, which is paramount in many sport activities [36–38]. It is a
213	                     product of force and velocity, but depending on how force and velocity are calculated, the
214	                     resultant “power output” can vary [30,36]. How force is calculated has a great impact on
215	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                           5 of 14
216	
217	
218	
219	                     the “power output”, producing contradictory findings that can confuse S&C coaches. For
220	                     example, studies that have analyzed the load that maximizes power output in different
221	                     exercises have found heterogenous results, with wide observed ranges (from 30 to 80%
222	                     1RM) that still make it challenging to come to a consensus about which load elicits the
223	                     maximal power output [30,39–42]. Likely, the main reason for those discrepancies is the
224	                     method used to calculate the force. The gold standard to measure force production in
225	                     dynamic actions, such as jumping or lifting, are force plates [30,43]; they are designed to
226	                     continuously measure force exerted on them, and calculate the force applied to the system
227	                     mass (e.g., the bodyweight of the athlete plus the mass of the barbell), when performing the
228	                     exercise. Most velocity tracking systems (e.g., linear transducers, accelerometers, MoCap)
229	                     do not take into account the athlete’s bodyweight (mass) in their “power” calculations;
230	                     therefore, reviewing whether they are included in the force calculation is advised). Instead,
231	                     they calculate it by the differentiation in the velocity measured to obtain acceleration, and
232	                     afterward multiply it to the mass of the barbell [41,43]. This method has been proven to
233	                     underestimate the actual power (force applied at a given velocity), when pushing to the
234	                     ground when jumping [44]. Studies using “barbell power” measurement have observed
235	                     that the load that maximizes power in vertical jumps, or ballistic bench press throws, are
236	                     much higher than those using the “system power” [36,41,45,46]. For example, if the body
237	                     mass (aka system mass) is considered in the calculation of force, the load that maximizes
238	                     power output is close to 0 kg (i.e., unloaded jump), while, when considering only the
239	                     barbell mass, the load that maximizes power output is close to 100% of body weight for
240	                     the external load [46]. Thus, the practical recommendation to maximize “power output”
241	                     during vertical jumping can be completely different if the system mass or the barbell mass
242	                     is used in the calculation of force. Although “barbell power output” could be of great
243	                     interest for athletes whose main activity is to apply maximum power to an implement
244	                     (e.g., throwing), it is our opinion that it is not the most appropriate method when assessing
245	                     power production capabilities in team sport players. Nonetheless, if the goal the S&C
246	                     coach is to measure “power output”, they are encouraged to use force platforms and
247	                     include the total mass (athlete body mass and external mass) in the computations from the
248	                     linear transducer.
249	                           Finally, it is worth noting that different manufacturers might report different velocity
250	                     metrics, with the most popular being MVC, mean concentric velocity of the propulsive
251	                     phase (MPV) and/or peak velocity (PV) [8,29,47]. While it has been proposed that MPV can
252	                     better represent the velocity production ability of the athlete [48], it has also been observed
253	                     that mean concentric velocity (MCV)is as reliable as MPV [47], and, from a technological
254	                     point of view, simpler to measure. It is also worth mentioning that, considering that MCV,
255	                     MPV and PV are different (generally, MCV < MPV < PV), these metrics should not be used
256	                     interchangeably. For standardization purposes, in this document we refer to MCV when
257	                     citing velocity of execution.
258	
259	                     4. Determination of Individual Load–Velocity Profiles in Team Sport
260	                          Early technology used to measure velocity was expensive, not accessible to the vast
261	                     majority of practitioners and mainly constrained to measure vertical motions (e.g., linear
262	                     transducers). Nowadays, there are more accessible devices, capable of measuring the
263	                     velocity in different types of equipment, which allow the assessment of numerous exercises
264	                     simultaneously (e.g., a player being able to track a session in multiple exercises or players
265	                     working at the same time in different stations). The latest point, working with large squads,
266	                     is probably one of the biggest challenges when it comes to measuring (or testing) in team
267	                     sports, since time can be a constraint. Velocity tracking systems are evolving, making
268	                     assessment procedures less time consuming for both coaches and players. However, there
269	                     are some key aspects to take into account to successfully implement VBT during the RT
270	                     session with team sport athletes.
271	                          The vast majority of the exercises analyzed in the VBT literature arebarbell-
272	                     based [8,49–51], and researchers have found an almost a perfect association between
273	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                6 of 14
274	
275	
276	
277	                     mean concentric velocity (MCV) and load (%1RM) in several exercises, such as bench-
278	                     press, back squat, deadlift or hip-thrust. Some studies have also observed that the load–
279	                     velocity relationship is well-fitted in machine and cable-based exercises (e.g., the leg
280	                     extension) [35]. What is important to highlight here is that the load–velocity relationship
281	                     is exercise-dependent [18,52,53], since the load that represents a certain absolute velocity
282	                     can vary greatly between exercises (Table 2). Thus, the use of absolute “velocity zones”
283	                     is discouraged, since a certain velocity (e.g., 1.0 m·s−1 ) can represent a low load (mass)
284	                     (e.g., when performing a back squat) or a near maximal load (e.g., when performing an
285	                     Olympic Snatch). Including a battery of one lower-body, one upper-body, and/or full body
286	                     multi-joint barbell exercises in the assessment is recommended.
287	
288	                     Table 2. Velocities for different %1RM from an individual load–velocity profile of one player, for
289	                     bench-press, back squat, deadlift and pull-up exercises [8,18,52,53].
290	
291

294	                          (% 1RM)

313	                           The load–velocity profile is created by calculating a regression that fits the veloc-
314	                     ity (data points) with different loads (absolute or relative), where the more loads as-
315	                     sessed, the higher the accuracy of the profile. However, including a high number of loads
316	                     (e.g., 10 loads) would be time consuming and impractical when testing a large squad of
317	                     players. Moreover, in order to avoid fatigue and guarantee that the athletes are performing
318	                     the lift at their maximal velocity capabilities, a passive rest of 3 to 5 min between loads is
319	                     needed. Consequently, it is recommended to select a number of loads (mass; data points)
320	                     that is time efficient but, at the same time, that guarantees a regression fit. It was observed
321	                     that profiles created from two loads can be as reliable as those created from six loads, as
322	                     long as the loads used are properly selected; in this case, it seems that a light load (about
323	                     40% 1RM) and a heavy load (about 80% 1RM) are the best options [11,54]. However, if
324	                     one of the two loads are not properly performed (i.e., athletes not applying their maxi-
325	                     mal intended velocity), the results can be drastically altered. Therefore, we recommend
326	                     performing between 4 and 6 sets with incremental loads to guarantee that the results are
327	                     reliable (Table 3).
328	                           Research has shown that subjective scales are highly related with MCV in different
329	                     resistance exercises [55–57]. For example, it has been observed that both the Repetitions in
330	                     Reserve (RIR) (calculated as the number or % of repetitions performed with respect to the
331	                     maximum number of possible repetitions) and the Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scores
332	                     are associated with velocity loss with different loads [58]. Hence, accounting for the RIR
333	                     and/or RPE can be useful tools when programming, and for understanding the mechanical
334	                     fatigue that the athlete is experiencing without having to measure the velocity drop over the
335	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                   7 of 14
336	
337	
338	
339	                     set. Moreover, it has been shown that the inclusion of RIR with the movement velocity in a
340	                     multiple regression improves the accuracy of the load–velocity profile [59]. While practitioners
341	                     should ideally measure MCV in most of the main exercises, prescribing RT using RIR can
342	                     be a suitable solution in those exercises where calculating the load–velocity profiles might
343	                     be of less interest or not suitable, such as dumbbell, cable, kettlebell exercises, and the like.
344	                     Moreover, it has been observed in youth basketball players that training using a RIR approach
345	                     is more suitable than conducting traditional repetitions to failure when velocity is not used to
346	                     monitor training load [60]. Table 4 presents a VBT training prescription where some exercises
347	                     are prescribed using velocity, and others are based on RIR.
348	
349	                     Table 3. Protocol to determine the load–velocity profile; bench press exercises as an example.
350	
351	                                      Loads selection: Select 4–6 incremental loads, using velocity as a reference, starting
352	                            1         approximately @ 30–40% 1RM (>1.15–1.20 m·s−1 ) and until approximately @

355	                            2         can be lifted approximately @ >1.20–1.25 m·s−1 . This set can be used to adjust the
356	                                      1st load for the incremental test.
357	                                      Set 1–4/6: Athlete performs 2 reps with each load (1 rep when using heavier loads is
358	                                      allowed), pushing the barbell as fast as possible. The fastest repetition is the one
359	                                      used for the calculations.

362	                                      needed. Rest ≈2–3 min between sets, ideally passively. Other interspersed exercises
363	                                      can be performed, but these should not involve upper body or fatigue.
364	                                      Load increment between sets: Ideally, the load should be increased similarly (for
365	                            4         example, by adding 5 or 10 kg in each new set, or a similar velocity lose), or a
366	                                      proportional decrease in velocity (≈0.10 m·s−1 ).

370	                                      the change in velocity for that particular load, and/or (ii) measure at a certain
