400	                     5. Considerations for a Successful Implementation of a Velocity-Based Program
401	                          The velocity of execution (during the concentric phase of dynamic exercises) is a key
402	                     training variable in sports performance. In the following, we present some important
403	                     remarks when implementing VBT:
404	                     •    The most relevant consideration when training based on the velocity of execution
405	                          (VBT) is that velocity must be the maximal intended. If the athlete does not perform
406	                          with a maximal intended velocity (regardless of the load (mass) or %1RM), the results
407	                          would be underestimated [61].
408	                     •    VBT is not specific for velocity-oriented sessions or exercises; it is a RT methodol-
409	                          ogy based on the velocity of execution, used to prescribe, monitor and analyze RT.
410	                          The velocity of execution can be used at different %RM (percentage-based training),
411	                          including heavy loads; choosing appropriate and key exercises is paramount.
412	                     •    While the 1RM might vary within days, the velocity at each 1RM percentage when
413	                          individual load–velocity profiles are computed is very stable [62]. Therefore, the
414	                          velocity of execution with a fixed absolute load can be a good indicator of effort and
415	                          actual (current) performance.
416	                     •    The velocity measured is both load (%RM) and exercise dependent. It has been shown
417	                          that different exercises have unique velocities associated with each percentage of the
418	                          1RM (Table 2).
419	                     •    Individual load–velocity profiles can differ between genders, age or training status [49,63],
420	                          and they have shown higher reliability than generalized profiles created from norma-
421	                          tive data [64,65].
422	                     •    Practitioners can benefit from combining objective and subjective scales to improve the
423	                          accuracy of the training load prescription. As observed in a recent review on the topic,
424	                          both objective (i.e., mean concentric velocity) and subjective measurements (i.e., repe-
425	                          titions in reserve) can help to enhance muscular strength by prescribing training loads
426	                          that take into account the athlete’s daily fluctuations in performance or fatigue [66].
427	                          Moreover, it has been observed that the combination of MCV and RIR increases the
428	                          accuracy of the 1RM estimation in comparison with using MCV alone [59].
429	                     •    The mean velocity might represent different levels of effort depending on the an-
430	                          thropometric profile. It is paramount to create individual load–velocity profiles for
431	                          each athlete, especially if the players within a team have large differences in their
432	                          anthropometrics. This can be especially relevant in sports like basketball, where limb
433	                          lengths can have a wide range between players. For example, two players can lift the
434	                          same relative load (i.e., %1RM) in the bench press at 0.8 m·s−1 , but player-A barbell’s
435	                          displacement is 0.35 m, while for player-B it is 0.6 m; this means that player-B has pro-
436	                          duced the same velocity as player-A, but in almost twice the time (0.75 s for player-B
437	                          vs. 0.43 s for player-A). Thus, player-B spends more time under tension, meaning that
438	                          the overall effort for the same velocity might be higher for player-B than for player-A.
439	
440	                     6. Prescribing and Monitoring Training Loads with VBT
441	                          There are certain methodological aspects when using velocity of execution during
442	                     RT that can be relevant as indicators of effort and for monitoring training on a daily basis.
443	                     As a starting point, practitioners could choose key exercises for the training cycle, and
444	                     determine a load–velocity profile for those. Secondly, the relative intensities of the training
445	                     cycle (e.g., %RM) should be defined. Thereafter, measure the velocity in the first set of an
446	                     exercises to establish subsequent loads for the day; to do that on a daily basis, practitioners
447	                     would choose a fixed load (mass) for the warm-up, perform one set of 1–2 repetitions and
448	                     measure the MCV. Once the velocity at the fixed load is known for that day/exercise, adjust
449	                     loads to the actual (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete that represents the
450	                     intended velocity for the programmed intensity (%RM). Figure 2 displays an example of a
451	                     player’s load–velocity profile, the speed for the warm-up repetition, and the corresponding
452	                     %RM. The faster the velocity, the lower the percentage of the 1RM that the load represents.

462	                                         Finally, prescribe the number of repetitions per set by either: (i) the velocity loss
463	                                  thresholds within the series, (ii) the repetitions in reserve, or (iii) using subjective scales. A
464	                                  relevant use of VBT when prescribing RT sessions is being able to identify neuromuscular
465	                                  fatigue and modify the number repetitions the athlete should perform during the set [10,67].
466	                                  It has been observed that velocity loss during the set is highly related with markers of
467	                                  fatigue such as lactate or ammonia [68]. Studies have observed that low velocity loss
468	                                  thresholds (i.e., 10–20% loss from the fastest repetition) can produce similar improvements
469	                                  in physical performance with significantly lower training volume than higher thresholds
470	                                  (i.e., 40% loss or more) [67,69] On the contrary, if the RT goal is to maximize muscle mass,
471	                                  research has shown that lifting close to muscular failure is more adequate [70,71], and it
472	                                  has been observed that high velocity loss thresholds (i.e., 40% or more, which means going
473	                                  closer to failure) would be more appropriate to increase hypertrophy [69].
474	                                         The goal of strength training in sport is to improve force, velocity and power output
475	                                  production capabilities [37]. A positive training program would change MCV with a fixed
476	                                  absolute load/s or the load that can be lifted at a fixed speed. It has been shown that load–
477	                                  velocity profiles (i.e., the velocity associated with each %1RM) can be altered after a period
478	                                  of training of 4 to 6 weeks [49,72]. Thus, it is recommended to re-assess the load–velocity
479	                                  profile every ≈4–6 weeks, or after specific cycles of RT, in order to evaluate the effects of
480	                                  the RT. However, the training capacity of the athlete might vary on a daily basis, and that
481	                                  is why the measurement of the velocity execution in the first series or repetitions of an
482	                                  exercise is useful for the programming of each training session. Some velocity tracking
483	                                  systems (e.g., My Lift App, Madrid, Spain) include calculations within their algorithms that
484	                                  estimate 1RM on a daily basis by measuring individual load–velocity profiles, as explained
485	                                  in Figure 2.

508	                                  7. Conclusions
509	                                        This manuscript aimed to provide a guideline to better implement VBT in team sport
510	                                  settings. The ultimate goal of RT in team sports is to improve the force production applied
511	                                  at a certain load (mass), at a given velocity and/or during a certain time. The velocity of
512	                                  execution is a reliable indicator of effort for programming and monitoring training, as well
513	                                  as for managing fatigue, both on a daily basis and in long term periodization.
514	                                        The advance in tracking systems allows measurement of an athlete’s velocity of
515	                                  execution during RT sessions, in different exercises during the same session, for a more
516	                                  comprehensive monitoring of the program. However, managing large squads during every
517	                                  training session can be challenging; how to best use technology in an efficient way, and
518	                                  educate coaches and players in its use, would be paramount.
519	                                        One consideration when using VBT tracking systems is the lack of research in their
520	                                  use in different strength training modalities, such as eccentric-overload training, pneumatic
521	                                  resistance or iso-inertial devices, and elastic-based equipment, where a velocity–effort
522	                                  (e.g., load (mass), %RM) relationship might not be the primary RT training goal with
523	                                  these tools.
524	 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                                11 of 14
525	
526	
527	
528	                                        Programming using VBT does not automatically imply programming effectively.
529	                                  The prescription, control, monitoring and evaluation of a RT using VBT requires a clear
530	                                  understanding of certain physics concepts, as well as strength training methodology. The
531	                                  VBT implementation should not be seen as an accessory to traditional RT or as a purely
532	                                  motivational tool for providing real-time feedback (the latter, without a doubt, being a great
533	                                  tool). The use of velocity in RT is a training paradigm, where specific strength goals and
534	                                  adaptations can be achieved by properly programming and tracking velocity of execution.
535	                                  It also allows for an objective quantification of the resistance training loads. Implementing
536	                                  VBT to monitor players’ performance can support decision-making processes, particularly
537	                                  the making of informed decisions when programing RT, and improvements in knowledge
538	                                  of the strength training paradigm.

The Implementation of Velocity-Based Training Paradigm for
Team Sports: Framework, Technologies, Practical
Recommendations and Challenges
Carlos Balsalobre-Fernández 1, *                 and Lorena Torres-Ronda 2,3

                                          1   Applied Biomechanics and Sports Technology Research Group, Autonomous University of Madrid,
                                              28049 Madrid, Spain
                                          2   Institute for Health & Sport, Victoria University, Melbourne, VIC 3011, Australia; lorenatorres07@yahoo.es
                                          3   Spanish National Basketball Federation, 28036 Madrid, Spain
                                          *   Correspondence: carlos.balsalobre@uam.es or info@carlos-balsalobre.com

                                          Abstract: While velocity-based training is currently a very popular paradigm to designing and
                                          monitoring resistance training programs, its implementation remains a challenge in team sports,
                                          where there are still some confusion and misinterpretations of its applications. In addition, in contexts
                                          with large squads, it is paramount to understand how to best use movement velocity in different
                                          exercises in a useful and time-efficient way. This manuscript aims to provide clarifications on the
                                          velocity-based training paradigm, movement velocity tracking technologies, assessment procedures
                                          and practical recommendations for its application during resistance training sessions, with the
                                          purpose of increasing performance, managing fatigue and preventing injuries. Guidelines to combine
                                          velocity metrics with subjective scales to prescribe training loads are presented, as well as methods
          

                                          1. Introduction

Sports 2021, 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.3390/sports9040047                                                       https://www.mdpi.com/journal/sports
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                            2 of 14



                     prescribe RT based on velocity of execution. This is a key element in most sport disciplines,
                     either by the requirements of the sport (e.g., sprinting, accelerating/decelerating, jumping,
                     throwing, kicking) or as an indicator of intensity (e.g., neuromuscular demands) [7,8].
                     There are reports of German weightlifters using linear transducers in the 1970s [9]. Since
                     that time, research on the benefits of lifting velocity to prescribe and monitor RT has
                     been conducted [8,10–12]. Being able to objectively monitor RT sessions, adapt the goals
                     individually, or provide feedback in real time on a daily basis is paramount, especially when
                     working with elite players. In addition, compiling information will allow a critical analysis
                     based on objective data on the implemented methodology, and thus enable the necessary
                     adjustments and advancements in the knowledge of the strength training theory. However,
                     there are still some confusion, misinterpretations and wrong practices when implementing
                     VBT in team sports. Therefore, the aim of this article is to provide a comprehensive
                     overview of the main benefits, technologies and best practices when implementing VBT
                     programs in team sports.

                     2. The Challenges and Drawbacks of the 1-Repetition Maximum Paradigm
                          The value of 1RM represents the maximal load (mass) that the athlete can lift, in a
                     concentric dynamic action, with proper form, once but not twice [13]. Thus, performing
                     a 1RM is considered a maximal dynamic effort. Once this value is known, programming
                     of RT is done prescribing relative loads to the individual’s 1RM [14,15]. However, this
                     methodology comes with certain disadvantages.
                          It is well known in the powerlifting community that experienced lifters are able
                     to move their 1RM load (mass) at a lower speed than their less trained or experienced
                     counterparts, especially in complex multi-joint exercises. Either due to inexperience, not
                     making a truly maximum effort or having experience but avoiding situations of risk of
                     injury using maximum loads, the 1RM is often poorly measured, which implies that the
                     consequent prescribed load (percentage-based training; nRM%), or velocities for each
                     1RM%, will not be adequate.
                          Moreover, as happens with other measures of physical performance, the 1RM could
                     vary on a daily basis due to several uncontrolled factors (e.g., fatigue, mental preparation,
                     sleep, stress or nutrition) [16]. Hence, in order to prescribe a precise load for each session,
                     the 1RM should be tested at the beginning of every RT session to adjust loads to the actual
                     (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete. However, since conducting an actual
                     1RM test before each training session is utopic, traditional percentage-based approaches
                     have been used, where the 1RM is assessed at the beginning of a training cycle, the %RM is
                     calculated and the RT program periodized for the subsequent weeks according to it [12,17].
                     The main drawback with this approach is that, since the actual 1RM could vary from
                     one session to another, the subsequent prescribed loads (mass) for the cycle would likely
                     represent a different effort to the initial loads (%RM) programed based on the original 1RM.
                     As an illustration of this potential discrepancy, Table 1 displays a RT load progression over
                     a period of 8-weeks, with one example based on the 1RM assessed prior to the training
                     cycle, and an example based on daily estimations using load–velocity profiles.
                          Additionally, the effort that represents each 1RM percentage differs between exer-
                     cises [18,19], where, for example, the 85% 1RM represents a different effort in bench press
                     vs. back squat. Furthermore, the load that represents a %1RM still requires performing
                     repetitions to failure, and extensive research has shown that performing repetitions to mus-
                     cular failure can impair performance, at specific times of a periodization program, due to an
                     excessive production of fatigue, thus making it inappropriate for team sports training [20].

      actual daily values.

      In the pretest session (i.e., Session 0), the 1RM of the athlete represented in this table was 130 kg in the bench-press exercise. Those 130 kg
      were used as a reference in the “pretest programming”, while daily 1RM scores estimated by measuring barbell velocity were used in the
      “daily programming”. Note that in the pre-test programming, every session would have been performed with 91 kg (i.e., the 70% of the
      pre-test 1RM), but if daily variations would have been taken into account, the actual load would have variated on a daily basis.


                                      3. Technologies to Track Velocity for Resistance Training
                                            Due to the growing interest in VBT, there has been a proliferation of devices measuring
                                      velocity for RT, from motion capture systems (MoCap), linear transducers and accelerome-
                                      ters, to low-cost smartphone apps. In addition, this phenomenon has been accompanied
                                      by a number of studies conducted on the validity and reliability of some of these novel
                                      technologies to measure velocity [21–29]. However, each of these technologies has advan-
                                      tages and disadvantages, and practitioners tasked with managing the systems have the
                                      responsibility to understand the pros and cons of the different systems, as well as using a
                                      systematic process in the data collection, being knowledgeable on best practices regarding
                                      implementing VBT, and applying critical thinking when assessing their RT methodologies.
                                            Team sports rarely require static, linear or single-joint movements. Rather, it is the
                                      opposite in that there are not only complex movements but also ones performed in highly
                                      unpredictable environments and with opponents (involving contact, perturbations, colli-
                                      sions, and such). Velocity tracking systems are still far from being able to measure with
                                      ecological validity; most are designed to measure traditional strength exercises, connected
                                      to equipment, or to certain body segments.
                                            Linear transducers are probably one of the most popular technologies used in the
                                      implementation of VBT to date. One of the downsides is that they are limited to measure
                                      vertical motion only [30,31]. Most commercial models available in the market just measure
                                      the vertical component of the velocity vector, meaning that any horizontal or lateral motion
                                      during the lift would be (and should be) omitted (Figure 1). Horizontal displacements
                                      do occur when using free weights even in “vertical” exercises like the back squat [32,33];
                                      hence, a proper exercise form and technique should be guaranteed, and exercises with a
                                      horizontal or angular momentum component avoided.
                                            In most cases, linear transducers are attached to one end of a barbell, and thus they
                                      actually register the velocity of that part of the bar, which could differ from the velocity
                                      of the other end if the athlete did not lift it perfectly, parallel to the ground. Lifting an
                                      unbalanced barbell does happen in practice, and S&C coaches using linear transducers
                                      should be aware of this fact. To reduce this type of error in the measurement, some studies
                                      have used two linear transducers, and reported the mean velocity registered from the two
                                      devices [30,32]. This may not be feasible in applied contexts; an alternative support may
                                      be having a visual control of the form of execution (objective or subjective) and exclude
                                      incorrect repetitions. It is then recommended that the device is placed consistently on the
                                      same side.
                                            Trying to solve some of the aforementioned limitations, different novel technologies
                                      such as accelerometers or smartphone apps have emerged as a cost-effective and prac-
                                      tical alternative to measure movement velocity in resistance exercises, and studies have
                                      shown that they can do it in a valid and reliable way [22,25,28,34]. For example, certain
                                      accelerometers can track velocity in exercises with horizontal displacement, while apps
                                      have shown reliable measurement of mean concentric velocity in cable-based exercises
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                   4 of 14



                     by video-recording the vertical ascent of the machine’s weight stack [35]. However, these
                     devices come with their own limitations. While they have shown moderate to good validity
                     and reliability, accelerometers had the lowest accuracy when compared with other devices,
                     such as linear transducers, apps, MoCap or gold-standard instruments [22,28]. A popular
                     app [25] has presented validity, reliability and accuracy higher than accelerometers; how-
                     ever, since it is video-based (frame-to-frame slow motion navigation), the measurements
                     are not provided in real time. When comparing different linear transducers, studies have
                     observed differences in absolute velocity outputs [28]. Thus, when interpreting VBT re-
                     search (especially when looking to raw velocity data) practitioners should interpret results
                     carefully; it is advised to not use devices from different manufactures interchangeably.




                     Figure 1. Generic linear transducer showing a deviation of 20◦ from the vertical during a lift.
                     For a registered mean velocity of 0.82 m·s−1 , the actual magnitude of the resultant mean velocity
                     vector would be 0.87 m/s, as calculated using simple trigonometry (Actual velocity = Registered
                     velocity/cos (angle). Most of the load–velocity relationships analyzed in the scientific literature are
                     conducted with exercises performed in Smith machines, since this equipment guarantees a complete
                     vertical motion of the barbell. This, however, reduces the ecological validity of the load–velocity
                     relationship itself, since these profiles can differ if the lift is performed with free weights (where
                     horizontal displacements occur) or with a Smith machine.

                           Another common misappropriation of technologies to track movement velocity is
                     its application for the measurement of power or “muscle power”. Power is important in
                     sport because it is an expression of performance, the consequence of the force applied in a
                     given time in a given action, which is paramount in many sport activities [36–38]. It is a
                     product of force and velocity, but depending on how force and velocity are calculated, the
                     resultant “power output” can vary [30,36]. How force is calculated has a great impact on
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                           5 of 14



                     the “power output”, producing contradictory findings that can confuse S&C coaches. For
                     example, studies that have analyzed the load that maximizes power output in different
                     exercises have found heterogenous results, with wide observed ranges (from 30 to 80%
                     1RM) that still make it challenging to come to a consensus about which load elicits the
                     maximal power output [30,39–42]. Likely, the main reason for those discrepancies is the
                     method used to calculate the force. The gold standard to measure force production in
                     dynamic actions, such as jumping or lifting, are force plates [30,43]; they are designed to
                     continuously measure force exerted on them, and calculate the force applied to the system
                     mass (e.g., the bodyweight of the athlete plus the mass of the barbell), when performing the
                     exercise. Most velocity tracking systems (e.g., linear transducers, accelerometers, MoCap)
                     do not take into account the athlete’s bodyweight (mass) in their “power” calculations;
                     therefore, reviewing whether they are included in the force calculation is advised). Instead,
                     they calculate it by the differentiation in the velocity measured to obtain acceleration, and
                     afterward multiply it to the mass of the barbell [41,43]. This method has been proven to
                     underestimate the actual power (force applied at a given velocity), when pushing to the
                     ground when jumping [44]. Studies using “barbell power” measurement have observed
                     that the load that maximizes power in vertical jumps, or ballistic bench press throws, are
                     much higher than those using the “system power” [36,41,45,46]. For example, if the body
                     mass (aka system mass) is considered in the calculation of force, the load that maximizes
                     power output is close to 0 kg (i.e., unloaded jump), while, when considering only the
                     barbell mass, the load that maximizes power output is close to 100% of body weight for
                     the external load [46]. Thus, the practical recommendation to maximize “power output”
                     during vertical jumping can be completely different if the system mass or the barbell mass
                     is used in the calculation of force. Although “barbell power output” could be of great
                     interest for athletes whose main activity is to apply maximum power to an implement
                     (e.g., throwing), it is our opinion that it is not the most appropriate method when assessing
                     power production capabilities in team sport players. Nonetheless, if the goal the S&C
                     coach is to measure “power output”, they are encouraged to use force platforms and
                     include the total mass (athlete body mass and external mass) in the computations from the
                     linear transducer.
                           Finally, it is worth noting that different manufacturers might report different velocity
                     metrics, with the most popular being MVC, mean concentric velocity of the propulsive
                     phase (MPV) and/or peak velocity (PV) [8,29,47]. While it has been proposed that MPV can
                     better represent the velocity production ability of the athlete [48], it has also been observed
                     that mean concentric velocity (MCV)is as reliable as MPV [47], and, from a technological
                     point of view, simpler to measure. It is also worth mentioning that, considering that MCV,
                     MPV and PV are different (generally, MCV < MPV < PV), these metrics should not be used
                     interchangeably. For standardization purposes, in this document we refer to MCV when
                     citing velocity of execution.

                     4. Determination of Individual Load–Velocity Profiles in Team Sport
                          Early technology used to measure velocity was expensive, not accessible to the vast
                     majority of practitioners and mainly constrained to measure vertical motions (e.g., linear
                     transducers). Nowadays, there are more accessible devices, capable of measuring the
                     velocity in different types of equipment, which allow the assessment of numerous exercises
                     simultaneously (e.g., a player being able to track a session in multiple exercises or players
                     working at the same time in different stations). The latest point, working with large squads,
                     is probably one of the biggest challenges when it comes to measuring (or testing) in team
                     sports, since time can be a constraint. Velocity tracking systems are evolving, making
                     assessment procedures less time consuming for both coaches and players. However, there
                     are some key aspects to take into account to successfully implement VBT during the RT
                     session with team sport athletes.
                          The vast majority of the exercises analyzed in the VBT literature arebarbell-
                     based [8,49–51], and researchers have found an almost a perfect association between
 Sports 2021, 9, 47                                                                                                6 of 14



                     mean concentric velocity (MCV) and load (%1RM) in several exercises, such as bench-
                     press, back squat, deadlift or hip-thrust. Some studies have also observed that the load–
                     velocity relationship is well-fitted in machine and cable-based exercises (e.g., the leg
                     extension) [35]. What is important to highlight here is that the load–velocity relationship
                     is exercise-dependent [18,52,53], since the load that represents a certain absolute velocity
                     can vary greatly between exercises (Table 2). Thus, the use of absolute “velocity zones”
                     is discouraged, since a certain velocity (e.g., 1.0 m·s−1 ) can represent a low load (mass)
                     (e.g., when performing a back squat) or a near maximal load (e.g., when performing an
                     Olympic Snatch). Including a battery of one lower-body, one upper-body, and/or full body
                     multi-joint barbell exercises in the assessment is recommended.

                     Table 2. Velocities for different %1RM from an individual load–velocity profile of one player, for
                     bench-press, back squat, deadlift and pull-up exercises [8,18,52,53].



                            Load
                          (% 1RM)



                             40%                1.03                1.21                 1                 0.93
                             45%                0.96                1.14               0.94                0.88
                             50%                0.89                1.06               0.87                0.83

                             95%                0.24                0.39               0.31                0.43
                            100%                0.17                0.32               0.25                0.38


                           The load–velocity profile is created by calculating a regression that fits the veloc-
                     ity (data points) with different loads (absolute or relative), where the more loads as-
                     sessed, the higher the accuracy of the profile. However, including a high number of loads
                     (e.g., 10 loads) would be time consuming and impractical when testing a large squad of
                     players. Moreover, in order to avoid fatigue and guarantee that the athletes are performing
                     the lift at their maximal velocity capabilities, a passive rest of 3 to 5 min between loads is
                     needed. Consequently, it is recommended to select a number of loads (mass; data points)
                     that is time efficient but, at the same time, that guarantees a regression fit. It was observed
                     that profiles created from two loads can be as reliable as those created from six loads, as
                     long as the loads used are properly selected; in this case, it seems that a light load (about
                     40% 1RM) and a heavy load (about 80% 1RM) are the best options [11,54]. However, if
                     one of the two loads are not properly performed (i.e., athletes not applying their maxi-
                     mal intended velocity), the results can be drastically altered. Therefore, we recommend
                     performing between 4 and 6 sets with incremental loads to guarantee that the results are
                     reliable (Table 3).
                           Research has shown that subjective scales are highly related with MCV in different
                     resistance exercises [55–57]. For example, it has been observed that both the Repetitions in
                     Reserve (RIR) (calculated as the number or % of repetitions performed with respect to the
                     maximum number of possible repetitions) and the Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scores
                     are associated with velocity loss with different loads [58]. Hence, accounting for the RIR
                     and/or RPE can be useful tools when programming, and for understanding the mechanical
                     fatigue that the athlete is experiencing without having to measure the velocity drop over the

                     5. Considerations for a Successful Implementation of a Velocity-Based Program
                          The velocity of execution (during the concentric phase of dynamic exercises) is a key
                     training variable in sports performance. In the following, we present some important
                     remarks when implementing VBT:
                     •    The most relevant consideration when training based on the velocity of execution
                          (VBT) is that velocity must be the maximal intended. If the athlete does not perform
                          with a maximal intended velocity (regardless of the load (mass) or %1RM), the results
                          would be underestimated [61].
                     •    VBT is not specific for velocity-oriented sessions or exercises; it is a RT methodol-
                          ogy based on the velocity of execution, used to prescribe, monitor and analyze RT.
                          The velocity of execution can be used at different %RM (percentage-based training),
                          including heavy loads; choosing appropriate and key exercises is paramount.
                     •    While the 1RM might vary within days, the velocity at each 1RM percentage when
                          individual load–velocity profiles are computed is very stable [62]. Therefore, the
                          velocity of execution with a fixed absolute load can be a good indicator of effort and
                          actual (current) performance.
                     •    The velocity measured is both load (%RM) and exercise dependent. It has been shown
                          that different exercises have unique velocities associated with each percentage of the
                          1RM (Table 2).
                     •    Individual load–velocity profiles can differ between genders, age or training status [49,63],
                          and they have shown higher reliability than generalized profiles created from norma-
                          tive data [64,65].
                     •    Practitioners can benefit from combining objective and subjective scales to improve the
                          accuracy of the training load prescription. As observed in a recent review on the topic,
                          both objective (i.e., mean concentric velocity) and subjective measurements (i.e., repe-
                          titions in reserve) can help to enhance muscular strength by prescribing training loads
                          that take into account the athlete’s daily fluctuations in performance or fatigue [66].
                          Moreover, it has been observed that the combination of MCV and RIR increases the
                          accuracy of the 1RM estimation in comparison with using MCV alone [59].
                     •    The mean velocity might represent different levels of effort depending on the an-
                          thropometric profile. It is paramount to create individual load–velocity profiles for
                          each athlete, especially if the players within a team have large differences in their
                          anthropometrics. This can be especially relevant in sports like basketball, where limb
                          lengths can have a wide range between players. For example, two players can lift the
                          same relative load (i.e., %1RM) in the bench press at 0.8 m·s−1 , but player-A barbell’s
                          displacement is 0.35 m, while for player-B it is 0.6 m; this means that player-B has pro-
                          duced the same velocity as player-A, but in almost twice the time (0.75 s for player-B
                          vs. 0.43 s for player-A). Thus, player-B spends more time under tension, meaning that
                          the overall effort for the same velocity might be higher for player-B than for player-A.

                     6. Prescribing and Monitoring Training Loads with VBT
                          There are certain methodological aspects when using velocity of execution during
                     RT that can be relevant as indicators of effort and for monitoring training on a daily basis.
                     As a starting point, practitioners could choose key exercises for the training cycle, and
                     determine a load–velocity profile for those. Secondly, the relative intensities of the training
                     cycle (e.g., %RM) should be defined. Thereafter, measure the velocity in the first set of an
                     exercises to establish subsequent loads for the day; to do that on a daily basis, practitioners
                     would choose a fixed load (mass) for the warm-up, perform one set of 1–2 repetitions and
                     measure the MCV. Once the velocity at the fixed load is known for that day/exercise, adjust
                     loads to the actual (current) daily maximal capabilities of the athlete that represents the
                     intended velocity for the programmed intensity (%RM). Figure 2 displays an example of a
                     player’s load–velocity profile, the speed for the warm-up repetition, and the corresponding
                     %RM. The faster the velocity, the lower the percentage of the 1RM that the load represents.

                                         Finally, prescribe the number of repetitions per set by either: (i) the velocity loss
                                  thresholds within the series, (ii) the repetitions in reserve, or (iii) using subjective scales. A
                                  relevant use of VBT when prescribing RT sessions is being able to identify neuromuscular
                                  fatigue and modify the number repetitions the athlete should perform during the set [10,67].
                                  It has been observed that velocity loss during the set is highly related with markers of
                                  fatigue such as lactate or ammonia [68]. Studies have observed that low velocity loss
                                  thresholds (i.e., 10–20% loss from the fastest repetition) can produce similar improvements
                                  in physical performance with significantly lower training volume than higher thresholds
                                  (i.e., 40% loss or more) [67,69] On the contrary, if the RT goal is to maximize muscle mass,
                                  research has shown that lifting close to muscular failure is more adequate [70,71], and it
                                  has been observed that high velocity loss thresholds (i.e., 40% or more, which means going
                                  closer to failure) would be more appropriate to increase hypertrophy [69].
                                         The goal of strength training in sport is to improve force, velocity and power output
                                  production capabilities [37]. A positive training program would change MCV with a fixed
                                  absolute load/s or the load that can be lifted at a fixed speed. It has been shown that load–
                                  velocity profiles (i.e., the velocity associated with each %1RM) can be altered after a period
                                  of training of 4 to 6 weeks [49,72]. Thus, it is recommended to re-assess the load–velocity
                                  profile every ≈4–6 weeks, or after specific cycles of RT, in order to evaluate the effects of
                                  the RT. However, the training capacity of the athlete might vary on a daily basis, and that
                                  is why the measurement of the velocity execution in the first series or repetitions of an
                                  exercise is useful for the programming of each training session. Some velocity tracking
                                  systems (e.g., My Lift App, Madrid, Spain) include calculations within their algorithms that
                                  estimate 1RM on a daily basis by measuring individual load–velocity profiles, as explained
                                  in Figure 2.

                                  7. Conclusions
                                        This manuscript aimed to provide a guideline to better implement VBT in team sport
                                  settings. The ultimate goal of RT in team sports is to improve the force production applied
                                  at a certain load (mass), at a given velocity and/or during a certain time. The velocity of
                                  execution is a reliable indicator of effort for programming and monitoring training, as well
                                  as for managing fatigue, both on a daily basis and in long term periodization.
                                        The advance in tracking systems allows measurement of an athlete’s velocity of
                                  execution during RT sessions, in different exercises during the same session, for a more
                                  comprehensive monitoring of the program. However, managing large squads during every
                                  training session can be challenging; how to best use technology in an efficient way, and
                                  educate coaches and players in its use, would be paramount.
                                        One consideration when using VBT tracking systems is the lack of research in their
                                  use in different strength training modalities, such as eccentric-overload training, pneumatic
                                  resistance or iso-inertial devices, and elastic-based equipment, where a velocity–effort
                                  (e.g., load (mass), %RM) relationship might not be the primary RT training goal with
                                  these tools.

                                        Programming using VBT does not automatically imply programming effectively.
                                  The prescription, control, monitoring and evaluation of a RT using VBT requires a clear
                                  understanding of certain physics concepts, as well as strength training methodology. The
                                  VBT implementation should not be seen as an accessory to traditional RT or as a purely
                                  motivational tool for providing real-time feedback (the latter, without a doubt, being a great
                                  tool). The use of velocity in RT is a training paradigm, where specific strength goals and
                                  adaptations can be achieved by properly programming and tracking velocity of execution.
                                  It also allows for an objective quantification of the resistance training loads. Implementing
                                  VBT to monitor players’ performance can support decision-making processes, particularly
                                  the making of informed decisions when programing RT, and improvements in knowledge
                                  of the strength training paradigm.

 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review, with no described search method, of how injury severity, pain, inflammation and psychological stress relate to sleep quality in soccer players. It draws mainly on cited studies from other populations, such as adolescents and general-population samples, and contains no original data. The authors report that injury-related pain and stress disturb sleep, and that poor sleep can slow recovery and raise reinjury risk.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search method, selection criteria or quality appraisal is described, so the choice of evidence cannot be checked. The reference list shows citations used for claims beyond their stated scope, for example a study of physical activity in virtual football players is cited for match injury incidence.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the proposed chain of injury, pain, sleep loss and reinjury as established, when the review offers no controlled outcome data for it.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Malliou VJ, Pafis G, Ispirlides I, Daskalaki K, Katsikas C. The impact of injury severity on sleep quality in soccer players. European Journal of Sport Sciences. 2025;4(3):1-8.",
   "doi": "10.24018/ejsport.2025.4.3.230",
   "abstract": "Reviews the literature on how injury severity relates to sleep quality in soccer players. Topics are pain and inflammation, psychological stress, effects of poor sleep on recovery and reinjury, and practical sleep strategies. The authors argue that sleep should be treated as a core part of injury rehabilitation.",
   "tldr": "This review argues that injury pain, inflammation and stress disturb sleep in soccer players, and that poor sleep can slow recovery and raise reinjury risk. It recommends building sleep assessment, sleep hygiene, relaxation and nutrition support into rehabilitation.",
   "methods": "Narrative review. The authors do not describe a search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal of study quality.",
   "findings": "The review groups the literature into pain and sleep, inflammatory responses, psychological stress, and long-term effects of poor sleep on recovery. Its conclusions are narrative and it reports no pooled estimates.",
   "limitations": "No systematic search, selection or quality appraisal is described. Some citations are used for claims beyond what the cited work covers, and soccer-specific evidence is not separated from general-population evidence.",
   "practicalImplications": "Sleep screening, consistent sleep schedules, pre-sleep routines and pain control are reasonable to include in post-injury plans, as the review suggests. The specific supplement and device suggestions are not supported by the review's own evidence.",
   "athleteDev": "Not a performance-development study. The sleep and recovery points may inform recovery planning for soccer players, but the review does not test performance outcomes.",
   "rtp": "The review supports including sleep assessment and sleep support in rehabilitation planning. It cannot show that sleep interventions shorten return to play or reduce reinjury, because it presents no controlled data on either outcome."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q02",
 "sourceFile": "The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective observational study of an entire national track cycling squad (n = 7; 3 men, 4 women) monitored with wrist actigraphy and daily sleep diaries from 5 days before to 5 days after long-haul eastward travel across 7 time zones. Actigraphy showed reduced time in bed, total sleep time and sleep efficiency, mostly in the 48 hours after arrival, and sleep diaries showed lower sleep quality and higher bedtime fatigue. The authors report that most measures returned toward baseline by day A+3.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Seven athletes from one squad, with no comparison group, no chronotype or performance data, and no sleep education or countermeasure arm, so travel effects cannot be separated from other fatigue. Some statistics cite n = 10, one section heading does not match its content, and one sleep-quality test has no printed p-value.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff might read the 48-hour disruption window as a validated rule for travel scheduling, when it comes from one small squad with no comparison group.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Doherty R, Madigan SM, Nevill A, Warrington G, Ellis JG. The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes. Neurobiology of Sleep and Circadian Rhythms. 2023;15:100102.",
   "doi": "10.1016/j.nbscr.2023.100102",
   "abstract": "Assessed sleep in seven elite national track cyclists (3 men, 4 women) before, during and after long-haul eastward travel, using actigraphy and daily sleep diaries. Time in bed, total sleep time and sleep efficiency fell with travel, mostly in the 48 hours after arrival, and bedtime fatigue rose. The authors recommend pairing sleep measures with chronotype and perceived sleep need.",
   "tldr": "In seven elite track cyclists, eastward long-haul travel cut time in bed, sleep time and sleep efficiency, mostly in the first 48 hours after arrival. Most measures were back near baseline by the third day after arrival, so plan the first two nights after arrival carefully.",
   "methods": "Prospective observational study of one national squad. Wrist actigraphy (ActiWatch 2) and the Consensus Sleep Diary were collected from 5 days before travel to 5 days after arrival, and analysed with mixed models, ANOVA and regression.",
   "findings": "Actigraphy showed time in bed reduced by 213 min on the travel day and 157 min on arrival day A+1, compared with other days. Total sleep time was reduced by 268 min on travel and 197 min on A+1, and sleep efficiency fell on both days. Sleep diaries showed lower time in bed, total sleep time and sleep quality during travel, with higher bedtime fatigue; awakenings and morning fatigue did not change significantly.",
   "limitations": "Only seven athletes, with no comparison group and no chronotype, performance or training data. Some statistics cite n = 10, the awakenings section reports WASO, and the sleep-quality test has no printed p-value. The discussion also cites a study of unfair p value wording as significant, so the discussion needs care.",
   "practicalImplications": "The authors' data support allowing time between arrival and competition, because sleep loss was greatest in the first 48 hours after arrival. The authors also suggest assessing chronotype and perceived sleep need alongside sleep measures before choosing individual interventions.",
   "athleteDev": "Shows that eastward long-haul travel reduced sleep time and time in bed for elite cyclists, which could affect training quality in the days after arrival. The study does not measure training or performance.",
   "rtp": "Not designed for return-to-sport decisions. It can inform sleep planning around competition travel, but it cannot show effects on injury, return to play or performance."
 }
}

 "id": "Q03",
 "sourceFile": "The impact of long-haul travel and 13 h time change on sleep and rest activity circadian rhythm in speed skaters during World Cup competitions.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The impact of long-haul travel and 13 h time change on sleep and rest activity circadian rhythm in speed skaters during World Cup competitions' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Female Athletes", "Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective observational study of 19 Canadian national short-track speed skaters (11 women) who travelled about 13 time zones to World Cup races in Asia in 2017 and 2019. Wrist actigraphy showed total sleep of 6 h 16 min during travel and 6 h 35 min on race days, against 7 h 08 min at baseline, then 7 h 32 min during the stay in Asia, with sleep rising about 9 minutes per night to day 5. Jump height was higher in Asia than at baseline, and race times did not differ from other races of the same season.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Actigraphy estimates sleep without polysomnography or a hypnogram, and no subjective sleep data were collected. The stay-in-Asia analysis pools two seasons and treats 2017 days 5 to 8 as day 5, and the jump data come from only 10 athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read recovery within five days as proof that travel plans are unnecessary, when the study had no comparison group or intervention arm.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2025,
   "citation": "Varesco G, Yao CW, Dubé E, Simonelli G, Bieuzen F. The impact of long-haul travel and 13 h time change on sleep and rest activity circadian rhythm in speed skaters during World Cup competitions. Experimental Physiology. 2025;110(11):1732-1743.",
   "doi": "10.1113/EP092195",
   "abstract": "Tracked sleep, rest-activity rhythms, jump height and race results in 19 Canadian short-track speed skaters who travelled about 13 time zones to World Cup races in Asia. Sleep was reduced during travel, increased during the stay in Asia and recovered within five days. Race results did not differ from other races in the same season.",
   "tldr": "Speed skaters who flew about 13 time zones slept less during travel, then slept more in Asia, with sleep rising about 9 minutes a night up to day 5. Race performance did not differ from other races that season.",
   "methods": "Prospective observational design across the 2017 and 2019 World Cups. Motionwatch 8 actigraphy was worn from one week before travel; rest-activity rhythms were estimated by cosinor analysis, and countermovement jump was measured by force plate in 10 athletes. Mixed-effects models compared phases, and a piecewise model located a change point at day 5.",
   "findings": "Total sleep time was 7 h 08 min at baseline, 6 h 16 min during travel, 6 h 35 min on race days and 7 h 32 min in Asia. In Asia, sleep efficiency (82.3% vs 81.0% at baseline, P = 0.007) and jump height (P = 0.0004) were higher than at baseline, and sleep time rose about 9 min per night to day 5 (P = 0.0002). Race times and rankings did not differ from other races of the same season.",
   "limitations": "Only 19 athletes, with actigraphy as the sleep measure and no subjective sleep or objective training-load data. The abstract gives P < 0.0001 for the day-5 sleep rise, but Table 2 gives P = 0.0002, and this summary uses the table value. The authors saw race results before starting the analysis, and the jump gains may reflect tapering or competition arousal, as the authors acknowledge.",
   "practicalImplications": "Athletes can be expected to recover sleep within about five days when given enough sleep opportunity and daily activity in the new time zone. The authors suggest that sleep opportunity and activity mattered more than timed light or melatonin, but this study did not compare those approaches.",
   "athleteDev": "Shows that speed skaters' sleep and activity rhythms adapted within about five days after a large time shift, with jump height higher in Asia, which may help plan training in the days after arrival. The study does not test any training programme.",
   "rtp": "Not built for return-to-sport decisions. It can inform travel recovery planning, but it does not measure injury, return to play or rehabilitation outcomes."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q04",
 "sourceFile": "The impact of non-operative hip and core injuries on NFL athlete performance.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Front matter reads 'The Impact of Non-Operative Hip and Core Injuries on National Football League Athlete Performance' with DOI 10.1080/00913847.2021.1976603, matching the filename. This is the accepted author version of the same article as Q05 (identical DOI); operator may dedupe.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective study of 112 NFL players (41 offensive, 71 defensive) with non-operative hip or core injuries from 2010 to 2016, compared with 224 matched controls (2:1) on age, position and NFL experience, using public records and power ratings. All injured players returned to play, missing a mean of 4.0 games (offence) and 3.1 games (defence). Defensive players played fewer games than controls two years after injury (9.5 vs 10.9, P = 0.04), while within-player pre-injury to post-injury declines were significant for defensive games and power rating and for offensive skill-player power rating.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Injury and performance data come from public sources that may be incomplete, injury diagnoses are not clinically verified, and power ratings omit linemen and kickers. The matched-control comparison is the stronger test, and it shows only one significant difference.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pre-to-post declines in games and power rating as caused by injury, when matched controls show no significant power-rating difference and the declines are within-player comparisons.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2021,
   "citation": "Tramer JS, Jildeh TR, Castle JP, Buckley P, Nowak C, Okoroha KR. The impact of non-operative hip and core injuries on National Football League athlete performance. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2021.",
   "doi": "10.1080/00913847.2021.1976603",
   "abstract": "Retrospective matched-control study of NFL players with non-operative hip or core injuries from 2010 to 2016. All injured players returned to play. Defensive players played fewer games than matched controls two years after injury, and both offensive and defensive players had lower power ratings after injury than in their own pre-injury careers.",
   "tldr": "NFL players with non-operative hip or core injuries all returned to play. Defensive players played fewer games than matched controls in the two years after injury, but power ratings did not differ from controls.",
   "methods": "Retrospective study using public injury reports and game statistics for 112 players with hip or core injury, each matched 2:1 to healthy rostered players by age, position, performance and experience. Offensive and defensive power ratings were calculated for the injury season and the two seasons either side. Groups were compared with t-tests, chi-square, paired tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.",
   "findings": "Offensive players missed 4.0 games and defensive players 3.1 games on average. Defensive players played fewer games at two years (9.5 vs 10.9, P = 0.04) but not cumulatively (37.5 vs 41.4, P = 0.16). Within-player declines were significant for defensive games (58.1 to 37.4) and defensive power rating (219.8 to 133.9), and for offensive skill-player power rating (341.8 to 205.7, P = 0.03). No power-rating difference from controls was significant.",
   "limitations": "Public-source data may be incomplete, injuries are not clinically confirmed, and power ratings omit linemen and kickers. The discussion says offensive players with core injuries played fewer cumulative games than controls, but no p-value or table supports this, and the conclusion says offensive players were unaffected, so the offensive findings are internally inconsistent.",
   "practicalImplications": "Return to play after non-operative hip or core injury was near universal in this sample, which can support reassurance when counselling players. Staff should expect defensive players to play fewer games in the two following years and monitor them for that.",
   "athleteDev": "Shows that defensive players lost games and power rating after hip or core injuries, relative to their own earlier careers, which can guide what to monitor after return. It does not test any training or rehabilitation method.",
   "rtp": "Supports the finding that most players return to play after non-operative hip and core injuries, and that defensive players may miss games for about two years. It cannot show which rehabilitation approach works, because treatment and clinical details were not available."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective observational study of an entire national track cycling squad (n = 7; 3 men, 4 women) monitored with wrist actigraphy and daily sleep diaries from 5 days before to 5 days after long-haul eastward travel across 7 time zones.  "synthesisCaution": "Staff might read the 48-hour disruption window as a validated rule for travel scheduling, when it comes from one small squad with no comparison group.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Doherty R, Madigan SM, Nevill A, Warrington G, Ellis JG. The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes. Neurobiology of Sleep and Circadian Rhythms. 2023;15:100102.",
   "doi": "10.1016/j.nbscr.2023.100102",
   "abstract": "Assessed sleep in seven elite national track cyclists (3 men, 4 women) before, during and after long-haul eastward travel, using actigraphy and daily sleep diaries. Time in bed, total sleep time and sleep efficiency fell with travel, mostly in the 48 hours after arrival, and bedtime fatigue rose. The authors recommend pairing sleep measures with chronotype and perceived sleep need.",
   "tldr": "In seven elite track cyclists, eastward long-haul travel cut time in bed, sleep time and sleep efficiency, mostly in the first 48 hours after arrival. Most measures were back near baseline by the third day after arrival, so plan the first two nights after arrival carefully.",
   "methods": "Prospective observational study of one national squad. Wrist actigraphy (ActiWatch 2) and the Consensus Sleep Diary were collected from 5 days before travel to 5 days after arrival, and analysed with mixed models, ANOVA and regression.",
   "findings": "Actigraphy showed time in bed reduced by 213 min on the travel day and 157 min on arrival day A+1, compared with other days. Total sleep time was reduced by 268 min on travel and 197 min on A+1, and sleep efficiency fell on both days. Sleep diaries showed lower time in bed, total sleep time and sleep quality during travel, with higher bedtime fatigue; awakenings and morning fatigue did not change significantly.",
   "limitations": "Only seven athletes, with no comparison group and no chronotype, performance or training data. Some statistics cite n = 10, the awakenings section reports WASO, and the sleep-quality test has no printed p-value. The discussion also cites a study of unfair p value wording as significant, so the discussion needs care.",
   "practicalImplications": "The authors' data support allowing time between arrival and competition, because sleep loss was greatest in the first 48 hours after arrival. The authors also suggest assessing chronotype and perceived sleep need alongside sleep measures before choosing individual interventions.",
   "athleteDev": "Shows that eastward long-haul travel reduced sleep time and time in bed for elite cyclists, which could affect training quality in the days after arrival. The study does not measure training or performance.",
   "rtp": "Not designed for return-to-sport decisions. It can inform sleep planning around competition travel, but it cannot show effects on injury, return to play or performance."

{
 "id": "Q06",
 "sourceFile": "The impact of sleep interventions on athletic performance - A systematic review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review' (Cunha et al.) matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA systematic review of sleep intervention studies in athletes. Searches of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science in May 2022 returned 1584 records, and 25 studies published 2011 to 2021 were included, with 9 to 31 athletes each across 17 sports. The authors report that naps and sleep extension had the most consistent benefits for performance, while sleep hygiene, removing electronic devices and cold water immersion showed no effect; no meta-analysis was performed.",
 "screeningLimitations": "None of the included studies was judged to be at low risk of bias, and most were small crossover trials in trained athletes. Interventions, sports, tests and athlete levels were heterogeneous, so the review cannot give firm effect sizes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may treat the sleep-extension and nap findings as firm targets for every athlete, when the authors state that the evidence is limited and most studies were small with uncertain bias.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Cunha LA, Costa JA, Marques EA, Brito J, Lastella M, Figueiredo P. The impact of sleep interventions on athletic performance: a systematic review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2023;9:58.",
   "doi": "10.1186/s40798-023-00599-z",
   "abstract": "PRISMA systematic review of 25 studies testing sleep interventions (naps, sleep extension, sleep hygiene, light, mindfulness, removing electronic devices, cold water immersion and combinations) and their effects on athletes' sleep and performance or recovery. Sleep extension and naps had the most consistent benefits. Sleep hygiene, removing devices and cold water immersion showed no effect, but these conclusions rest on few studies.",
   "tldr": "Naps and extra night sleep (about 46 to 113 minutes over 3 to 49 nights) improved physical or cognitive performance in most athletes studied. Sleep hygiene, removing screens and cold water immersion showed no benefit in the few studies that tested them.",
   "methods": "PRISMA and PICOS review. Searches of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were run in May 2022; two reviewers screened independently with a third for disagreements, and risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 (crossover and randomized trials) and RoBANS (non-randomized studies).",
   "findings": "Of 1584 records, 25 studies were included: 60% crossover trials, 8% randomized controlled trials and 32% non-randomized studies. Naps improved cognitive performance in most studies, though physical results were mixed. Sleep extension improved reaction time and sport-specific performance in every study that tested it. Light therapy and mindfulness gave promising results from single studies. No included study was rated low risk of bias.",
   "limitations": "No included study was judged to be at low risk of bias, and many were small crossover trials. The review reports heterogeneity in interventions, sports, tests and athlete level, and it included only English-language studies.",
   "practicalImplications": "For athletes who usually sleep about 7 hours and feel they need more, extending sleep toward 9 to 10 hours in bed may be worth trying, and a 20 to 90 minute nap can supplement a short night. The authors advise allowing at least 30 minutes after a nap before performing, to limit sleep inertia.",
   "athleteDev": "Suggests that extra sleep or planned naps can improve reaction time, skill and some physical performance, which could be built into training weeks and tournament schedules. Effects on training adaptation were not studied.",
   "rtp": "Not designed for return to sport. The review includes no injury or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot show that sleep interventions speed rehabilitation or reduce reinjury."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q07",
 "sourceFile": "The impact of test loads on the accuracy of 1RM prediction using the load-velocity relationship.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The impact of test loads on the accuracy of 1RM prediction using the load-velocity relationship' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Validation study in 12 recreational weight trainers (body mass 80.8 kg, 1RM 84 kg) who had a direct Smith machine bench press 1RM test, then three bench press throws at each of 30 to 70% of 1RM, from which load-velocity regressions were fitted. The 30, 40 and 50% of 1RM model using peak velocity gave the best prediction (R2 0.96, SSE 4.2 kg) but under-predicted 1RM by about 9 kg and differed significantly from measured 1RM (P < 0.001). Mean-velocity models had R2 0.85 to 0.89 and no significant difference from measured 1RM, with Bland-Altman concerns about accuracy.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Twelve recreational lifters tested on a braked Smith machine, with no between-session reliability test, so the results do not transfer to free weights or athletes. The abstract presents the peak-velocity model as the most accurate, but the results report a significant difference from measured 1RM and a fixed bias of about 9 kg.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the 30 to 50% peak-velocity model as a precise 1RM estimate, when it carries a fixed bias of about 9 kg and differed significantly from measured 1RM.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2018,
   "citation": "Sayers MGL, Schlaeppi M, Hitz M, Lorenzetti S. The impact of test loads on the accuracy of 1RM prediction using the load-velocity relationship. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2018;10:9.",
   "doi": "10.1186/s13102-018-0099-z",
   "abstract": "Compared combinations of three submaximal bench press throw loads (30 to 70% of 1RM) for predicting Smith machine bench press 1RM in 12 recreational weight trainers, and compared models using mean versus peak bar velocity. The best model used peak velocity at 30, 40 and 50% of 1RM, with R2 of 0.96 and an SSE of 4.2 kg.",
   "tldr": "In 12 recreational lifters, a peak-velocity model built from three light bench press throws (30, 40 and 50% of 1RM) predicted Smith machine 1RM closely, but consistently underestimated it by about 9 kg. Treat it as a rough estimate rather than an exact 1RM.",
   "methods": "Smith machine bench press 1RM was measured directly in 12 recreational weight trainers. Two to three days later, a linear position transducer recorded mean and peak bar velocity during three bench press throws at each of 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70% of 1RM. Load-velocity regressions were built for three load windows and checked with repeated-measures ANOVA, Bland-Altman plots, CV and ICC.",
   "findings": "The 30 to 50% model using peak velocity had ICC 0.967 and R2 0.96 (SSE 4.2 kg), with a fixed bias of about 9 kg underestimation, and its predicted 1RM differed significantly from measured 1RM (P < 0.001). Mean-velocity models had R2 0.85 to 0.89 and no significant difference from measured 1RM (P = 0.21 to 0.95), but Bland-Altman plots showed accuracy concerns. Peak-velocity values were more reliable than mean-velocity values at most loads.",
   "limitations": "Small sample of recreational lifters, bench press throws on a Smith machine only, no between-session reliability test, and predictions outside the tested load range are not valid. The abstract calls the peak-velocity model the most accurate, but the results show a significant difference from measured 1RM and a 9 kg bias, so the abstract overstates accuracy.",
   "practicalImplications": "A light test of three bench press throws at 30 to 50% of 1RM can give a rough 1RM estimate for recreational lifters without a maximal lift, provided the roughly 9 kg underestimate is allowed for. Staff should not apply this to free-weight testing or to athletes without further validation.",
   "athleteDev": "Offers a low-load way to estimate Smith machine bench press 1RM and to track strength change in recreational or novice lifters. It is not validated for athletes, free weights or other exercises.",
   "rtp": "Not for return-to-sport decisions. The study included healthy people only, did not test injured or rehabilitating individuals, and did not compare injury or soreness rates with traditional testing, so it cannot show the method is safe or accurate in those groups."
 }
}

It covers limits of 1RM testing, the errors of bar-velocity technologies, load-velocity profiling with 4 to 6 incremental loads (with R2 above 0.92 as a quality check in the authors' experience), combining velocity with RIR or RPE, velocity-loss thresholds, and monitoring trends. The paper cites a named commercial app and gives a personal-domain contact, yet declares no conflicts of interest, so device examples should be read as illustrative.",
