 "paper": {
   "year": 2021,
   "citation": "Balsalobre-Fernández C, Torres-Ronda L. The implementation of velocity-based training paradigm for team sports: framework, technologies, practical recommendations and challenges. Sports. 2021;9:47.",
   "doi": "10.3390/sports9040047",
   "abstract": "Sets out a framework for velocity-based training in team sports, covering the limits of 1RM testing, technologies for measuring bar velocity, load-velocity profiling, combining velocity with subjective scales, daily 1RM estimation and monitoring. It flags limits such as the vertical-only measurement of many devices, the misuse of velocity-based power, and individual variation.",
   "tldr": "Velocity-based training can guide daily load and fatigue decisions in large team-sport squads if athletes lift with maximal intent and each athlete's load-velocity profile is measured. Device choice and power calculations need care, because the velocity recorded depends on both.",
   "methods": "Narrative review and practical framework with no described search strategy. The authors combine cited studies with applied experience, and an illustrative 8-week example.",
   "findings": "The paper argues that load-velocity profiles are exercise-specific and individual, can be built from 4 to 6 incremental loads, and can be used with a fixed-load warm-up repetition to judge the day's 1RM. It notes that linear transducers measure only the vertical component, and that power calculated from barbell mass alone misrepresents jumping. It recommends combining velocity with RIR or RPE and using velocity-loss thresholds to manage fatigue.",
   "limitations": "The review is narrative, with no systematic selection of studies. The authors note that tracking systems have little research in eccentric-overload, pneumatic and elastic training. Their examples are illustrative, not data from a study.",
   "practicalImplications": "Build a profile for key lifts from 4 to 6 incremental loads, re-check it every 4 to 6 weeks, and use RIR or RPE for exercises where a profile is not practical. Keep device placement consistent and avoid mixing devices from different manufacturers.",
   "athleteDev": "Gives coaches a framework to prescribe and monitor strength work across large squads with time-efficient velocity testing, plus cautions on what velocity and power metrics mean. The paper presents no outcome data on performance gains.",
   "rtp": "The paper is about strength training in team sports, and it states an aim of preventing injuries, but it gives no return-to-play or injury data. It cannot establish that velocity-based training shortens rehabilitation or lowers reinjury risk."
 }
}

 "id": "Q05",
 "sourceFile": "The impact of nonoperative hip and core injuries on National Football League athlete performance.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The impact of nonoperative hip and core injuries on National Football League athlete performance' matches the filename. This is the final published version (51:1, 27-32) of the same article as Q04 (identical DOI); operator may dedupe.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective study of 112 NFL players (41 offensive, 71 defensive) with nonoperative hip or core injuries from 2010 to 2016, compared with 224 matched controls (2:1) on age, position and NFL experience, using public records and power ratings. All injured players returned to play, missing a mean of 4.0 games (offence) and 3.1 games (defence). Defensive players played fewer games than controls two years after injury (9.5 vs 10.9, P = 0.04), while within-player pre-injury to post-injury declines were significant for defensive games and power rating and for offensive skill-player power rating.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Injury and performance data come from public sources that may be incomplete, injury diagnoses are not clinically verified, and power ratings omit linemen and kickers. The matched-control comparison is the stronger test, and it shows only one significant difference.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pre-to-post declines in games and power rating as caused by injury, when matched controls show no significant power-rating difference and the declines are within-player comparisons.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Tramer JS, Jildeh TR, Castle JP, Buckley P, Nowak C, Okoroha KR. The impact of nonoperative hip and core injuries on National Football League athlete performance. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2023;51(1):27-32.",
   "doi": "10.1080/00913847.2021.1976603",
   "abstract": "Retrospective matched-control study of NFL players with nonoperative hip or core injuries from 2010 to 2016. All injured players returned to play. Defensive players played fewer games than matched controls two years after injury, and both offensive and defensive players had lower power ratings after injury than in their own pre-injury careers.",
   "tldr": "NFL players with nonoperative hip or core injuries all returned to play. Defensive players played fewer games than matched controls in the two years after injury, but power ratings did not differ from controls.",
   "methods": "Retrospective study using public injury reports and game statistics for 112 players with hip or core injury, each matched 2:1 to healthy rostered players by age, position, performance and experience. Offensive and defensive power ratings were calculated for the injury season and the two seasons either side. Groups were compared with t-tests, chi-square, paired tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.",
   "findings": "Offensive players missed 4.0 games and defensive players 3.1 games on average. Defensive players played fewer games at two years (9.5 vs 10.9, P = 0.04) but not cumulatively (37.5 vs 41.4, P = 0.16). Within-player declines were significant for defensive games (58.1 to 37.4) and defensive power rating (219.8 to 133.9), and for offensive skill-player power rating (341.8 to 205.7, P = 0.03). No power-rating difference from controls was significant.",
   "limitations": "Public-source data may be incomplete, injuries are not clinically confirmed, and power ratings omit linemen and kickers. The discussion says offensive players with core injuries played fewer cumulative games than controls, but no p-value or table supports this, and the conclusion says offensive players were unaffected, so the offensive findings are internally inconsistent.",
   "practicalImplications": "Return to play after nonoperative hip or core injury was near universal in this sample, which can support reassurance when counselling players. Staff should expect defensive players to play fewer games in the two following years and monitor them for that.",
   "athleteDev": "Shows that defensive players lost games and power rating after hip or core injuries, relative to their own earlier careers, which can guide what to monitor after return. It does not test any training or rehabilitation method.",
   "rtp": "Supports the finding that most players return to play after nonoperative hip and core injuries, and that defensive players may miss games for about two years. It cannot show which rehabilitation approach works, because treatment and clinical details were not available."
 }
}
